 وَلِهَذَا نَهَى عَنْهُمَا جَمِيعًا فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{وَلَا تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ}
 فَإِنَّهُ مَنْ لَبَّسَ الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ فَغَطَّاهُ بِهِ فَغَلِطَ بِهِ لَزِمَ أَنْ يَكْتُمَ الْحَقَّ الَّذِي تَبَيَّنَ أَنَّهُ بَاطِلٌ؛ إذْ لَوْ بَيَّنَهُ زَالَ الْبَاطِلُ الَّذِي لَبِسَ بِهِ الْحَقُّ. فَهَكَذَا مُشَاقَّةُ الرَّسُولِ وَاتِّبَاعُ غَيْرِ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَمَنْ شَاقَّهُ فَقَدْ اتَّبَعَ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِهِمْ وَهَذَا ظَاهِرٌ وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِهِمْ فَقَدْ شَاقَّهُ أَيْضًا؛ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ جَعَلَ لَهُ مُدْخَلًا فِي الْوَعِيدِ فَدَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ وَصْفٌ مُؤَثِّرٌ فِي الذَّمِّ فَمَنْ خَرَجَ عَنْ إجْمَاعِهِمْ فَقَدْ اتَّبَعَ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِهِمْ قَطْعًا وَالْآيَةُ تُوجِبُ ذَمَّ ذَلِكَ.
 وَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 هِيَ إنَّمَا ذِمَّتُهُ مَعَ مُشَاقَّةِ الرَّسُولِ.
 قُلْنَا:
 لِأَنَّهُمَا مُتَلَازِمَانِ وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ كُلَّ مَا أَجْمَعَ عَلَيْهِ الْمُسْلِمُونَ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ مَنْصُوصًا عَنْ الرَّسُولِ فَالْمُخَالِفُ لَهُمْ مُخَالِفٌ لِلرَّسُولِ كَمَا أَنَّ الْمُخَالِفَ لِلرَّسُولِ مُخَالِفٌ لِلَّهِ وَلَكِنْ هَذَا يَقْتَضِي أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا أَجْمَعَ عَلَيْهِ قَدْ بَيَّنَهُ الرَّسُولُ؛ وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّوَابُ.
translated_text:
in them all. Whoever disbelieves in the angels disbelieves in the Books and the messengers, and thus disbelieves in Allah, since he has denied His messengers and His Books. Likewise, whoever disbelieves in the Last Day denies the Books and the messengers, and is therefore a disbeliever.

The same applies to His words:

“O People of the Book, why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth knowingly?”

He censures them for both qualities. Each warrants censure, and the two are inseparable. Thus He forbids both together in His words:

“Do not mix truth with falsehood or conceal the truth knowingly.”

For whoever confounds truth with falsehood, covering it with falsehood and thereby falling into error, necessarily conceals the truth that has come to appear false. Were he to make it clear, the falsehood with which the truth was obscured would disappear.

The same applies to opposing the Messenger and following a path other than that of the believers. Whoever opposes him has followed a path other than theirs—this is evident. Whoever follows a path other than theirs has likewise opposed him. For He has made this a ground for the threatened punishment, showing that it is a factor warranting censure. Whoever departs from their consensus has unquestionably followed a path other than theirs, and the verse establishes that this deserves censure.

If it is said, “The verse only censures this when it is accompanied by opposition to the Messenger,” we reply: “That is because the two are inseparable.” Everything upon which the Muslims have reached consensus has been explicitly stated by the Messenger. Whoever opposes them therefore opposes the Messenger, just as whoever opposes the Messenger opposes Allah. This, however, entails that everything upon which consensus has been reached has been explained by the Messenger—and this is indeed correct.

original_text:
فَلَا يُوجَدُ قَطُّ مَسْأَلَةٌ مُجْمَعٌ عَلَيْهَا إلَّا وَفِيهَا بَيَانٌ مِنْ الرَّسُولِ وَلَكِنْ قَدْ يَخْفَى ذَلِكَ عَلَى بَعْضِ النَّاسِ وَيَعْلَمُ الْإِجْمَاعَ.
 فَيَسْتَدِلُّ بِهِ كَمَا أَنَّهُ يَسْتَدِلُّ بِالنَّصِّ مَنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ دَلَالَةَ النَّصِّ وَهُوَ دَلِيلٌ ثَانٍ مَعَ النَّصِّ كَالْأَمْثَالِ الْمَضْرُوبَةِ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَكَذَلِكَ الْإِجْمَاعُ دَلِيلٌ آخَرُ كَمَا يُقَالُ:
 قَدْ دَلَّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَالْإِجْمَاعُ وَكُلٍّ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأُصُولِ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَقِّ مَعَ تَلَازُمِهَا؛ فَإِنَّ مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْإِجْمَاعُ فَقَدْ دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَمَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ فَعَنْ الرَّسُولِ أُخِذَ فَالْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ كِلَاهُمَا مَأْخُوذٌ عَنْهُ وَلَا يُوجَدُ مَسْأَلَةٌ يَتَّفِقُ الْإِجْمَاعُ عَلَيْهَا إلَّا وَفِيهَا نَصٌّ. وَقَدْ كَانَ بَعْضُ النَّاسُ يَذْكُرُ مَسَائِلَ فِيهَا إجْمَاعٌ بِلَا نَصٍّ كَالْمُضَارَبَةِ وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ بَلْ الْمُضَارَبَةُ كَانَتْ مَشْهُورَةً بَيْنَهُمْ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ لَا سِيَّمَا قُرَيْشٌ؛
 فَإِنَّ الْأَغْلَبَ كَانَ عَلَيْهِمْ التِّجَارَةُ وَكَانَ أَصْحَابُ الْأَمْوَالِ يَدْفَعُونَهَا إلَى الْعُمَّالِ وَرَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَدْ سَافَرَ بِمَالِ غَيْرِهِ قَبْلَ النُّبُوَّةِ كَمَا سَافَرَ بِمَالِ خَدِيجَةَ وَالْعِيرُ الَّتِي كَانَ فِيهَا أَبُو سُفْيَانَ كَانَ أَكْثَرُهَا مُضَارَبَةً مَعَ أَبِي سُفْيَانَ وَغَيْرِهِ فَلَمَّا جَاءَ الْإِسْلَامُ أَقَرَّهَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَكَانَ أَصْحَابُهُ يُسَافِرُونَ بِمَالِ غَيْرِهِمْ مُضَارَبَةً وَلَمْ يَنْهَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَالسُّنَّةُ:
 قَوْلُهُ وَفِعْلُهُ وَإِقْرَارُهُ. فَلَمَّا أَقَرَّهَا كَانَتْ ثَابِتَةً بِالسُّنَّةِ.
translated_text:
Thus, there is never a matter on which consensus has been reached without an explanation from the Messenger concerning it. Some people, however, may be unaware of that explanation while knowing of the consensus. They therefore cite the consensus as evidence, just as someone who does not understand a text’s import may cite that text as evidence. This constitutes a second proof alongside the text, like the parables set forth in the Quran. Consensus likewise provides another proof, as when it is said: “This is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus.”

Each of these foundations points to the truth, and they are inseparably connected. Whatever consensus establishes is also established by the Book and the Sunnah. Whatever the Quran establishes has been received from the Messenger; thus, both the Book and the Sunnah are received from him. There is no matter on which consensus has been reached without a text concerning it.

Some people have cited matters on which there is consensus but supposedly no text, such as mudāraba (profit-sharing investment partnerships). This is not so. Rather, mudāraba was widely known among them in the pre-Islamic era, especially among Quraysh, whose predominant occupation was trade. Owners of capital would entrust their wealth to those who conducted business with it. Before his prophethood, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, travelled on trading journeys with other people’s wealth, including that of Khadījah. Most of the goods in the caravan accompanied by Abū Sufyān were held under mudāraba arrangements with Abū Sufyān and others.

When Islam came, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, approved this practice. His Companions would travel with other people’s wealth under mudāraba arrangements, and he did not prohibit it. The Sunnah comprises his sayings, actions, and tacit approvals. Since he approved this practice, it was established by the Sunnah.

original_text:
وَالْأَثَرُ الْمَشْهُورُ فِيهَا عَنْ عُمَرَ الَّذِي رَوَاهُ مَالِكٌ فِي الْمُوَطَّأِ وَيَعْتَمِدُ عَلَيْهِ الْفُقَهَاءُ لَمَّا أَرْسَلَ أَبُو مُوسَى بِمَالٍ أَقْرَضَهُ لِابْنَيْهِ وَاتَّجَرَا فِيهِ وَرَبِحَا وَطَلَبَ عُمَرُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ الرِّبْحَ كُلَّهُ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ لِكَوْنِهِ خَصَّهُمَا بِذَلِكَ دُونَ سَائِرِ الْجَيْشِ فَقَالَ لَهُ أَحَدُهُمَا:
 لَوْ خَسِرَ الْمَالَ كَانَ عَلَيْنَا فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ لَك الرِّبْحُ وَعَلَيْنَا الضَّمَانُ؟
 فَقَالَ لَهُ بَعْضُ الصَّحَابَةِ:
 اجْعَلْهُ مُضَارِبًا فَجَعَلَهُ مُضَارَبَةً وَإِنَّمَا قَالَ ذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ الْمُضَارَبَةَ كَانَتْ مَعْرُوفَةً بَيْنَهُمْ وَالْعَهْدَ بِالرَّسُولِ قَرِيبٌ لَمْ يَحْدُثْ بَعْدَهُ فَعَلِمَ أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ مَعْرُوفَةً بَيْنَهُمْ عَلَى عَهْدِ الرَّسُولِ كَمَا كَانَتْ الْفِلَاحَةُ وَغَيْرُهَا مِنْ الصِّنَاعَاتِ كَالْخِيَاطَةِ وَالْجِزَارَةِ. وَعَلَى هَذَا فَالْمَسَائِلُ الْمُجْمَعُ عَلَيْهَا قَدْ تَكُونُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْمُجْتَهِدِينَ لَمْ يَعْرِفُوا فِيهَا نَصًّا فَقَالُوا فِيهَا بِاجْتِهَادِ الرَّأْيِ الْمُوَافِقِ لِلنَّصِّ لَكِنْ كَانَ النَّصُّ عِنْدَ غَيْرِهِمْ.
 وَابْنُ جَرِيرٍ وَطَائِفَةٌ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَا يَنْعَقِدُ الْإِجْمَاعُ إلَّا عَنْ نَصٍّ نَقَلُوهُ عَنْ الرَّسُولِ مَعَ قَوْلِهِمْ بِصِحَّةِ الْقِيَاسِ.
 وَنَحْنُ لَا نَشْتَرِطُ أَنْ يَكُونُوا كُلُّهُمْ عَلِمُوا النَّصَّ فَنَقَلُوهُ بِالْمَعْنَى كَمَا تُنْقَلُ الْأَخْبَارُ لَكِنْ اسْتَقْرَأْنَا مَوَارِدَ الْإِجْمَاعِ فَوَجَدْنَاهَا كُلَّهَا مَنْصُوصَةً وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ النَّصَّ وَقَدْ وَافَقَ الْجَمَاعَةُ كَمَا أَنَّهُ قَدْ يَحْتَجُّ بِقِيَاسٍ وَفِيهَا إجْمَاعٌ لَمْ يَعْلَمْهُ فَيُوَافِقُ الْإِجْمَاعَ وَكَمَا يَكُونُ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ نَصٌّ خَاصٌّ وَقَدْ اسْتَدَلَّ فِيهَا بَعْضُهُمْ بِعُمُومِ كَاسْتِدْلَالِ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَغَيْرِهِ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{وَأُولَاتُ الْأَحْمَالِ أَجَلُهُنَّ أَنْ يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ}
 وَقَالَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ:
translated_text:
The well-known report from ʿUmar concerning this, narrated by Mālik in al-Muwattaʾ and relied upon by the jurists, relates that Abū Mūsā sent some money which he had lent to ʿUmar’s two sons. They traded with it and made a profit. ʿUmar demanded that the entire profit be taken for the Muslims, because Abū Mūsā had singled them out for this loan rather than the rest of the army. One of them said to him:

“Had the money been lost, we would have borne the loss. How, then, can you have the profit while we bear the liability?”

One of the Companions said to him:

“Treat him as the managing partner in a mudāraba.”

So he treated the transaction as a mudāraba. That Companion said this only because mudāraba was already familiar among them, and the Messenger’s time was still recent; it had not arisen after him. He therefore knew that it had been familiar among them during the Messenger’s lifetime, just as farming and other occupations, such as tailoring and butchery, had been.

Accordingly, in matters on which consensus has been reached, some jurists exercising independent judgment may have known of no relevant text and arrived at their conclusions through reasoning that agreed with the text, while other scholars possessed that text.

Ibn Jarīr and a group of scholars say:

“Consensus can only be established on the basis of a text they have transmitted from the Messenger.”

They maintain this while also affirming the validity of analogical reasoning.

We do not stipulate that they must all have known the text and conveyed its meaning, as reports are transmitted. Rather, we have surveyed the matters on which consensus has been reached and found that all of them are addressed by texts. Many scholars were unaware of the relevant text yet agreed with the body of scholars. Likewise, a scholar may argue by analogy in a matter on which there is a consensus unknown to him, and thus agree with that consensus. Similarly, a matter may be addressed by a specific text, while some scholars argue for it on the basis of a text’s general wording, as Ibn Masʿūd and others did when citing His words:

“For those who are pregnant, their waiting period is until they give birth.”

Ibn Masʿūd said:

original_text:
سُورَةُ النِّسَاءِ الْقُصْرَى نَزَلَتْ بَعْد الطُّولَى أَيْ:
 بَعْدَ الْبَقَرَةِ؛
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 
{أَجَلُهُنَّ أَنْ يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ}
 يَقْتَضِي انْحِصَارَ الْأَجَلِ فِي ذَلِكَ فَلَوْ أَوْجَبَ عَلَيْهَا أَنْ تَعُدَّ بِأَبْعَدَ الْأَجَلَيْنِ لَمْ يَكُنْ أَجْلُهَا أَنْ تَضَعَ حَمْلَهَا وَعَلِيٌّ وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ وَغَيْرُهُمَا أَدْخَلُوهَا فِي عُمُومِ الْآيَتَيْنِ وَجَاءَ النَّصُّ الْخَاصُّ فِي قِصَّةِ سبيعة الأسلمية بِمَا يُوَافِقُ قَوْلَ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ لَمَّا تَنَازَعُوا فِي الْمُفَوَّضَةِ إذَا مَاتَ زَوْجُهَا:
 هَلْ لَهَا مَهْرُ الْمِثْلِ؟
 أَفْتَى ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ فِيهَا بِرَأْيِهِ أَنَّ لَهَا مَهْرَ الْمِثْلِ ثُمَّ رَوَوْا حَدِيثَ بروع بِنْتِ وَاشِقٍ بِمَا يُوَافِقُ ذَلِكَ وَقَدْ خَالَفَهُ عَلِيٌّ وَزَيْدٌ وَغَيْرُهُمَا فَقَالُوا:
 لَا مَهْرَ لَهَا. فَثَبَتَ أَنَّ بَعْضَ الْمُجْتَهِدِينَ قَدْ يُفْتِي بِعُمُومٍ أَوْ قِيَاسٍ وَيَكُونُ فِي الْحَادِثَةِ نَصٌّ خَاصٌّ لَمْ يَعْلَمْهُ فَيُوَافِقُهُ وَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَسْأَلَةً وَاحِدَةً اتَّفَقُوا عَلَى إنَّهُ لَا نَصَّ فِيهَا؛
 بَلْ عَامَّةُ مَا تَنَازَعُوا فِيهِ كَانَ بَعْضُهُمْ يَحْتَجُّ فِيهِ بِالنُّصُوصِ أُولَئِكَ احْتَجُّوا بِنَصٍّ كَالْمُتَوَفَّى عَنْهَا الْحَامِلُ وَهَؤُلَاءِ احْتَجُّوا بِشُمُولِ الْآيَتَيْنِ لَهَا وَالْآخَرِينَ قَالُوا:
 إنَّمَا يَدْخُلُ فِي آيَةِ الْحَمْلِ فَقَطْ وَأَنَّ آيَةَ الشُّهُورِ فِي غَيْرِ الْحَامِلِ كَمَا أَنَّ آيَةَ الْقُرُوءِ فِي غَيْرِ الْحَامِلِ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ لَمَّا تَنَازَعُوا فِي الْحَرَامِ احْتَجَّ مَنْ جَعَلَهُ يَمِينًا بِقَوْلِهِ:
 {لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ
translated_text:
“The shorter surah on women was revealed after the longer one”—that is, after al-Baqara.

His words,

“their waiting period is until they give birth,”

mean that the waiting period ends at childbirth alone. If she were required to observe the longer of the two waiting periods, her waiting period would not end simply upon giving birth. ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and others included her within the general scope of both verses. Yet the specific text concerning the case of Subayʿa al-Aslamiyya supported Ibn Masʿūd’s position.

Likewise, when they disagreed over whether a woman married without a stipulated dowry was entitled to the customary dowry for a woman of her standing if her husband died, Ibn Masʿūd ruled, on the basis of his own judgment, that she was entitled to it. They subsequently narrated the hadith of Birwaʿ bint Wāshiq, which supported that ruling. ʿAlī, Zayd and others, however, disagreed with him, saying that she was entitled to no dowry.

It is thus established that a jurist exercising independent judgment may issue a ruling based on a text’s general wording or on analogy, while a specific text concerning the case, unknown to him, agrees with his ruling. No single case is known in which they agreed that there was no relevant text. Rather, in most matters over which they disagreed, some of them cited scriptural texts as evidence. Some appealed to a text, as in the case of a pregnant widow; others argued that both verses encompassed her. The opposing group maintained that she came under the verse concerning pregnancy alone, and that the verse specifying months applied to women who were not pregnant, just as the verse specifying menstrual cycles applied to women who were not pregnant.

each of them spoke according to the knowledge he possessed. Whoever discerned evidence in the Book cited it, and whoever discerned evidence in the Balance cited it. Sound proofs do not contradict one another, but some scholars may fail to perceive how they agree, or fail to recognize the weakness of one of them.

The Companions had an understanding of the Quran that eludes most later scholars, just as they knew aspects of the Sunnah and the Messenger’s circumstances that most later scholars do not know. They witnessed the Messenger and the revelation, saw him firsthand, and knew things about his words, deeds, and circumstances from which they could establish their conclusions—things unknown to most later scholars. Lacking that knowledge, these later scholars sought rulings through what they regarded as consensus or analogy.

Any later scholar who says, “Consensus is the basis of most of the Sharia,” is merely describing his own situation: his deficient knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah has made him dependent on it. This resembles their statement, “Most cases require analogy because the scriptural texts provide no indication of their rulings.” Such a statement comes only from someone unfamiliar with the Book and the Sunnah and how they indicate rulings.

Imam Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—said that there is no question that the Companions did not address, either directly or through a comparable case. When lands were conquered and Islam spread, every category of human activity presented itself, and they addressed these matters on the basis of the Book and the Sunnah. Only in a few questions did some of them speak on the basis of reasoned opinion. Most of them did not invoke consensus as evidence, nor did they need it, for they themselves were the people whose agreement constituted consensus; there was no consensus before them. Another version reads: “Then according to what the people have agreed upon.” Umar gave precedence to the Book, then the Sunnah. Likewise, Ibn Masʿūd said the same as he did. Umar gave precedence to the Book, then the Sunnah, then consensus. Similarly, Ibn Abbās would issue fatwas according to the Book, then the Sunnah, then the practice of Abū Bakr and Umar, in accordance with the Prophet’s words:

“Follow the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and Umar.”

These reports are established from Umar, Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn Abbās, who were among the Companions best known for issuing fatwas and judgments. This is the correct approach.

However, a group of later scholars said: “The scholar exercising independent judgment should begin by examining consensus. If he finds it, he should pay no attention to anything else. If he finds a scriptural text that contradicts it, he should believe that it was abrogated by a text that has not reached him.” Some of them said: “Consensus abrogated it.”

The correct approach, however, is that of the early generations. For if a scriptural text contradicts consensus, there must be a text supporting that consensus which establishes that the former text has been abrogated. As for the possibility that the Muslim community has lost the unabrogated text while preserving the abrogated one, this never occurs. It would mean attributing to the community the preservation of what it was forbidden to follow and the loss of what it was commanded to follow, whereas it is protected from that. Moreover, ascertaining consensus may frequently—or usually—be impossible. For who is there who

translated_text:
knows all the opinions of the scholars who exercise independent judgment? Scriptural texts, by contrast, can readily be known.

They judged according to the Book first because the Sunnah does not abrogate the Book. Nothing in the Quran, therefore, is abrogated by the Sunnah; rather, if anything in it is abrogated, the text that abrogates it is also in the Quran. One therefore gives nothing else precedence over the Quran. If one does not find the ruling there, one then seeks it in the Sunnah. Nothing in the Sunnah is abrogated except by the Sunnah itself: neither consensus nor anything else abrogates the Sunnah, nor may consensus be set against it.

Most versions of these reports say, “If he does not find it.” A person seeking a ruling may not find it in the Sunnah even though it is there; the same applies to the Quran. Thus, if one does not find it in the Quran, one may seek it in the Sunnah. If it is in the Sunnah, what the Sunnah contains will not contradict what is in the Quran. Likewise, sound consensus contradicts neither the Book nor the Sunnah.

Completed, with praise to Allah and by His help. May His blessings and peace be upon the best of His creation, Muhammad, and his family.

The following points should be noted:

First: These pages are extracted from the Shaykh’s discussion—may Allah have mercy on him—in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/83–125.

Second: There are nearly twenty minor differences between the two texts, most of which do not affect the meaning. The most important are:

1. At 19/205: “Sin is, in reality, an indication weightier than another.” The word al-ithm (“sin”) is a textual corruption; the correct reading is wa-lā thamma (“nor is there”), as in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/85.

2. At 19/212: “Because they based their position on the two aforementioned views concerning the view of the Qadariyya … and the view of the Jahmiyya.” The correct reading is: “The two aforementioned views: the view of the Qadariyya … and the view of the Jahmiyya,” as in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/212.

3. At 19/227: “And he did not know that praying with tayammum (dry ablution) was permissible, like Abū Dharr, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, and ‘Ammār when he entered a state of major ritual impurity.” The correct reading is: “Like Abū Dharr, and ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb and ‘Ammār when they both entered a state of major ritual impurity,” as in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/125.

Third: Whoever extracted this discussion from Minhāj al-Sunnah omitted certain passages from the Shaykh’s text. Some omissions were indicated by expressions such as “He goes on to say,” while others were not indicated. The details are as follows:

1. At 19/212: “Unbelief and grave disobedience are classifications established by revelation, not judgments that reason can establish independently.
He goes on to say: Accordingly, if error concerning rational questions said to constitute the foundations of religion amounts to unbelief …”

I say: The omitted discussion here extends from 5/92 to 5/95.

2. At 19/213: “The fundamental premise shared by both groups is that an agent possessing power and choice gives preference to one of two equivalent alternatives without a determining factor”—and so on to the end of what he quoted, may Allah have mercy on him. He then said: “This makes clear the third position concerning this fundamental issue …”

I say: The omitted discussion here extends from 5/96 to 5/98.

3. At 19/215: “Whoever has received no warner will not enter the Fire. And He said: ‘That is because your Lord would not destroy towns unjustly while their inhabitants were unaware’—that is, this is for that reason.”

I say: Three pages separate “will not enter the Fire” from his quotation of the verse: 5/100–103.

4. At 19/216: “It also indicates that this is an injustice from which He, glorified be He, is exalted. Furthermore, Allah Most High has stated in several places that He does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

I say: Seven pages separate “an injustice from which Allah, glorified be He, is exalted” from “Furthermore …”: 5/103–110.

Fourth: It appears to me that some passages quoted from the Shaykh contain omissions (1), as follows:

1. At 19/215–216: “It is thus established that He does not punish someone who is unaware unless a warner has come to him. It also indicates that this is an injustice from which He, glorified be He, is exalted.”

After “a warner,” the following words have been omitted: “How much more, then, must this apply to a child who lacks reason?” They appear in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/103. This omission may have been deliberate.

2. At 19/220: “No one says that Jews and Christians, after embracing Islam, emigrating, and joining the ranks of the Muslim emigrants who strive in Allah’s cause, are described as People of the Book—that is, as belonging to them—when they have believed in the Messenger.”

After “People of the Book,” the following passage has been omitted: “Just as one does not say of the Companions who were formerly polytheists, ‘Among the polytheists are those who believe in Allah and His Messenger,’ since after believing they were no longer called polytheists. This indicates that these are people belonging to the People of the Book—that is, counted among them …” This appears in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/115. It seems to me that this omission resulted from the copyist’s eye skipping from the first occurrence of “People of the Book” to the second. Allah knows best.

3. At 19/221: “Some said that it concerns the believers among the People of the Book. This is equivalent to the first view; if he intends it generally, it is equivalent to the second.”

After “People of the Book,” the following words have been omitted: “Among the Jews and Christians. If by this he means someone outwardly counted among the People of the Book, this is equivalent to the first view …” This appears in Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/117. This omission is like the preceding one.

Fifth: At 19/220, the text reads: “As Allah Most High said concerning someone killed by mistake: ‘And if he belonged to a people with whom you have a treaty,’ through to His words, ‘hostile to you, while he was a believer, then a believing slave must be freed’ …”

The editor of Minhāj al-Sunnah, 5/115, pointed out that this reading occurs in two manuscript copies but not the others, and that it is erroneous because it contradicts the order of the noble verse. End of quotation.

The correct reading is: “But if he belonged to a people hostile to you, while he was a believer, then a believing slave must be freed.”

There are three views on this fundamental issue, each held by a group of theoretical thinkers:

This is the well-known position of the Qadariyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. It is also the position of a group of speculative theologians outside these groups. They further say:

As for theoretical questions, there is conclusive evidence by which their truth can be known. Anyone who fails to ascertain it has therefore not expended his utmost effort in seeking the truth and thus incurs sin.

As for practical questions of religious law, they hold two positions:

The first is that these are like theoretical questions: there is conclusive evidence concerning every question, and anyone who goes against it incurs sin. Those who hold this position say that only one person is correct in any foundational or subsidiary question, and everyone other than the person who is correct incurs sin because he is mistaken. Some of them have said:

“Fundamental matters concern knowledge and belief, requiring only knowledge and belief, whereas subsidiary matters concern practice and require action.”

They said:

“This distinction is invalid. Some practical matters are such that denying them constitutes disbelief—for example, the obligation of the five daily prayers, zakat, and fasting the month of Ramadan, and the prohibition of unlawful sexual intercourse, usury, injustice, and indecencies.

“Conversely, there are matters of knowledge in which those who disagree incur no sin. Examples include the Companions’ disagreement over whether Muhammad saw his Lord; their disagreement concerning certain reports—whether the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, actually said something, and what he meant by it; their disagreement over whether certain words belong to the Quran; and their disagreement concerning certain meanings of the Quran and Sunnah—whether Allah and His Messenger intended such-and-such. Likewise, people disagree over the subtleties of speculative theology, such as the indivisible atom, the likeness of bodies, the persistence of accidents, and similar matters. Such disagreements do not warrant declaring anyone a disbeliever or an evildoer.”

They said:

“Practical matters involve both action and knowledge. If errors in these matters are forgiven, then errors in matters involving knowledge alone, without action, are all the more deserving of forgiveness.”

Others have said:

“Fundamental matters are those supported by conclusive evidence, while subsidiary matters are those not supported by conclusive evidence.”

The others replied:

“This distinction is also mistaken. Many practical matters are supported by evidence that is conclusive to those acquainted with it, while others are unaware of it. Some are conclusive by consensus, such as the prohibition of forbidden acts and the binding nature of evident obligations. Yet if someone denies them out of ignorance and on the basis of a mistaken interpretation, he is not declared a disbeliever until the proof has been established against him. Thus, during the time of ʿUmar, a group of people, including Qudāma, considered drinking wine lawful and believed it was permissible for them. The Companions did not declare them disbelievers before explaining their error to them, whereupon they repented and recanted. During the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, some people ate after dawn had broken until they could distinguish a white thread from a black thread. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not deem them sinful, let alone declare them disbelievers, although their error was beyond doubt.

“Likewise, Usāma ibn Zayd killed a Muslim man, and his error was beyond doubt. The same applies to those who found a man among his sheep. He said, ‘I am a Muslim,’ but they killed him and took his property. Their error was beyond doubt. Likewise, Khālid ibn al-Walīd killed members of Banū Jadhīma and took their property; he was unquestionably mistaken. The same applies to those who performed dry ablution up to their armpits, and to ʿAmmār, who rolled in the dust because he was in a state of major ritual impurity, just as an animal rolls. Indeed, those who entered a state of major ritual impurity and neither performed dry ablution nor prayed were also unquestionably mistaken. During the time of ʿUmar, a woman committed fornication. When she confessed, ʿUthmān said, “She speaks of it as openly as someone who does not know that it is forbidden.” When it became clear to the Companions that she knew it was forbidden, they did not subject her to the prescribed punishment. Yet considering fornication lawful is unquestionably an error.

If a man swears to something, believing it to be as he has sworn, and it then proves otherwise, he is unquestionably mistaken, but there is consensus that he bears no sin. Likewise, according to the majority, no expiation is required of him. Someone who eats believing that dawn still remains is unquestionably mistaken if it becomes clear to him that he ate after dawn. He bears no sin, though there is disagreement over whether he must make up the fast. The same applies to someone who believes that the sun has set, only for it to prove otherwise. There are many such examples.

Concerning Allah Most High’s words in the Quran:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake,”

Allah Most High said:

“I have done so.”

He made no distinction between an unquestionable error in a matter established conclusively and one in a matter established on probable evidence. As for a probable error, one cannot be certain that it is an error unless the person has unquestionably erred.

They said: “Whoever says that someone who makes a mistake in a matter established conclusively or on probable evidence thereby sins has contradicted the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations.”

قَالُوا:
 وَأَيْضًا فَكَوْنُ الْمَسْأَلَةِ قَطْعِيَّةً أَوْ ظَنِّيَّةً هُوَ أَمْرٌ إضَافِيٌّ بِحَسَبِ حَالِ الْمُعْتَقِدِينَ لَيْسَ هُوَ وَصْفًا لِلْقَوْلِ فِي نَفْسِهِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ قَدْ يَقْطَعُ بِأَشْيَاءَ عَلِمَهَا بِالضَّرُورَةِ؛ أَوْ بِالنَّقْلِ الْمَعْلُومِ صِدْقُهُ عِنْدَهُ وَغَيْرُهُ لَا يَعْرِفُ ذَلِكَ لَا قَطْعًا وَلَا ظَنًّا. وَقَدْ يَكُونُ الْإِنْسَانُ ذَكِيًّا قَوِيَّ الذِّهْنِ سَرِيعَ الْإِدْرَاكِ فَيَعْرِفُ مِنْ الْحَقِّ وَيَقْطَعُ بِهِ مَا لَا يَتَصَوَّرُهُ غَيْرُهُ وَلَا يَعْرِفُهُ لَا عِلْمًا وَلَا ظَنًّا.
 فَالْقَطْعُ وَالظَّنُّ يَكُونُ بِحَسَبِ مَا وَصَلَ إلَى الْإِنْسَانِ مِنْ الْأَدِلَّةِ وَبِحَسَبِ قُدْرَتِهِ عَلَى الِاسْتِدْلَالِ وَالنَّاسِ يَخْتَلِفُونَ فِي هَذَا وَهَذَا فَكَوْنُ الْمَسْأَلَةِ قَطْعِيَّةً أَوْ ظَنِّيَّةً لَيْسَ هُوَ صِفَةً مُلَازِمَةً لِلْقَوْلِ الْمُتَنَازَعِ فِيهِ حَتَّى يُقَالَ:
 كُلُّ مَنْ خَالَفَهُ قَدْ خَالَفَ الْقَطْعِيَّ بَلْ هُوَ صِفَةٌ لِحَالِ النَّاظِرِ الْمُسْتَدِلِّ الْمُعْتَقِدِ وَهَذَا مِمَّا يَخْتَلِفُ فِيهِ النَّاسُ فَعَلِمَ أَنَّ هَذَا الْفَرْقَ لَا يَطَّرِدُ وَلَا يَنْعَكِسُ.
 وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ فَرَّقَ بِفَرْقِ ثَالِثٍ وَقَالَ:
 الْمَسَائِلُ الْأُصُولِيَّةُ هِيَ الْمَعْلُومَةُ بِالْعَقْلِ فَكُلُّ مَسْأَلَةٍ عِلْمِيَّةٍ اسْتَقَلَّ الْعَقْلُ بِدَرْكِهَا فَهِيَ مِنْ مَسَائِلِ الْأُصُولِ الَّتِي يَكْفُرُ أَوْ يَفْسُقُ مُخَالِفُهَا.
 وَالْمَسَائِلُ الفروعية هِيَ الْمَعْلُومَةُ بِالشَّرْعِ قَالُوا:
 فَالْأَوَّلُ كَمَسَائِلِ الصِّفَاتِ وَالْقَدَرِ؛ وَالثَّانِي كَمَسَائِلِ الشَّفَاعَةِ وَخُرُوجِ أَهْلِ الْكَبَائِرِ مِنْ النَّارِ.
translated_text:
They said:

“Furthermore, whether a matter is certain or probable is relative to the circumstances of those who hold the belief; it is not a property of the proposition itself. A person may be certain of things that he knows self-evidently, or through reports whose truth is established for him, while someone else has neither certain nor probable knowledge of them. A person may also be intelligent, sharp-minded, and quick to understand, grasping truths with certainty that another person cannot even conceive of and has neither certain nor probable knowledge of.

“Certainty and probability thus depend on the evidence that has reached a person and his ability to reason from it. People differ in both respects. Whether a matter is certain or probable is therefore not an inherent property of the disputed proposition, such that one could say, ‘Everyone who disagrees with it has contradicted something certain.’ Rather, it describes the condition of the person examining the matter, reasoning about it, and holding the belief. This varies from one person to another. It is thus clear that this distinction does not hold consistently in either direction.”

Some of them drew a third distinction, saying:

“Fundamental matters are those known through reason. Every question concerning knowledge that reason can apprehend independently is therefore a fundamental matter, disagreement with which renders a person an unbeliever or a transgressor. Subsidiary matters are those known through revelation.”

They said: “The first category includes questions concerning the divine attributes and decree; the second includes questions concerning intercession and the departure from Hell of those who committed major sins.”

original_text:
فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ:
 مَا ذَكَرْتُمُوهُ بِالضِّدِّ أَوْلَى فَإِنَّ الْكُفْرَ وَالْفِسْقَ أَحْكَامٌ شَرْعِيَّةٌ لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَحْكَامِ الَّتِي يَسْتَقِلُّ بِهَا الْعَقْلُ.
 إلَى أَنْ قَالَ:
 وَحِينَئِذٍ فَإِنْ كَانَ الْخَطَأُ فِي الْمَسَائِلِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ الَّتِي يُقَالُ: إنَّهَا أُصُولُ الدِّينِ كُفْرًا فَهَؤُلَاءِ السَّالِكُونَ هَذِهِ الطُّرُقَ الْبَاطِلَةَ فِي الْعُقَلِ الْمُبْتَدَعَةِ فِي الشَّرْعِ هُمْ الْكُفَّارُ لَا مَنْ خَالَفَهُمْ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ الْخَطَأُ فِيهَا كُفْرًا فَلَا يَكْفُرُ مَنْ خَالَفَهُمْ فِيهَا فَثَبَتَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ كَافِرًا فِي حُكْمِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ عَلَى التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ وَلَكِنْ مِنْ شَأْنِ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ أَنَّهُمْ يَبْتَدِعُونَ أَقْوَالًا يَجْعَلُونَهَا وَاجِبَةً فِي الدِّينِ بَلْ يَجْعَلُونَهَا مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ الَّذِي لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ وَيُكَفِّرُونَ مَنْ خَالَفَهُمْ فِيهَا وَيَسْتَحِلُّونَ دَمَهُ كَفِعْلِ الْخَوَارِجِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة وَالرَّافِضَةِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ. وَأَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ لَا يَبْتَدِعُونَ قَوْلًا وَلَا يُكَفِّرُونَ مَنْ اجْتَهَدَ فَأَخْطَأَ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُخَالِفًا لَهُمْ مُسْتَحِلًّا لِدِمَائِهِمْ كَمَا لَمْ تُكَفِّرْ الصَّحَابَةُ الْخَوَارِجَ مَعَ تَكْفِيرِهِمْ لِعُثْمَانِ وَعَلِيٍّ وَمَنْ وَالَاهُمَا وَاسْتِحْلَالِهِمْ لِدِمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ الْمُخَالِفِينَ لَهُمْ. وَكَلَامُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسَائِلِ بِالتَّصْوِيبِ وَالتَّخْطِئَةِ وَالتَّأْثِيمِ وَنَفْيِهِ وَالتَّكْفِيرِ وَنَفْيِهِ؛ لِكَوْنِهِمْ بَنَوْا عَلَى الْقَوْلَيْنِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَيْنِ فِي قَوْلِ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ يَجْعَلُونَ كُلَّ مُسْتَدِلٍّ قَادِرًا عَلَى مَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِّ
translated_text:
They may therefore be told:

“The reverse of what you have stated is more appropriate, for classifying someone as an unbeliever or a transgressor is a matter of revealed law, not a judgment that reason can reach independently.”

Later, he said:

“Accordingly, if error in rational questions said to constitute the fundamentals of religion amounts to unbelief, then those who follow these methods—which are rationally unsound and religious innovations—are the unbelievers, not those who disagree with them. If error in these questions does not amount to unbelief, then those who disagree with them are not unbelievers. Thus, on either assumption, their opponent is not an unbeliever according to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger.

“Yet it is characteristic of the people of innovation to invent doctrines that they make obligatory in religion. Indeed, they make them an indispensable part of faith, declare anyone who disagrees with them an unbeliever, and deem it lawful to shed his blood. Such is the conduct of the Khawārij, the Jahmiyyah, the Rāfidah, the Muʿtazilah, and others.

“The people of the Sunnah, however, do not invent doctrines, nor do they declare someone an unbeliever for exercising independent judgment and reaching an erroneous conclusion, even if he opposes them and considers it lawful to shed their blood. Likewise, the Companions did not declare the Khawārij unbelievers, despite the latter’s declaring ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and their supporters unbelievers and considering it lawful to shed the blood of Muslims who disagreed with them.

“What these speculative theologians say concerning these questions—judging people correct or mistaken, sinful or free of sin, unbelievers or not unbelievers—stems from their reliance on the two positions mentioned earlier: the position of the Qadariyyah, who hold that everyone who reasons from evidence is capable of knowing the truth

original_text:
فَيُعَذَّبُ كُلُّ مَنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْهُ؛
 وَقَوْلُ الْجَهْمِيَّة الْجَبْرِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَا قُدْرَةَ لِلْعَبْدِ عَلَى شَيْءٍ أَصْلًا بَلْ اللَّهُ يُعَذِّبُ بِمَحْضِ الْمَشِيئَةِ فَيُعَذِّبُ مَنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْ ذَنْبًا قَطُّ وَيُنَعِّمُ مَنْ كَفَرَ وَفَسَقَ وَقَدْ وَافَقَهُمْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَقُولُونَ:
 يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُعَذِّبَ الْأَطْفَالَ وَالْمَجَانِينَ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْعَلُوا ذَنْبًا قَطُّ ثُمَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَجْزِمُ بِعَذَابِ أَطْفَالِ الْكُفَّارِ فِي الْآخِرَةِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُجَوِّزُهُ وَيَقُولُ: لَا أَدْرِي مَا يَقَعُ؟ وَهَؤُلَاءِ يُجَوِّزُونَ أَنْ يُغْفَرَ لِأَفْسَقِ أَهْلِ الْقِبْلَةِ بِلَا سَبَبٍ أَصْلًا وَيُعَذِّبُ الرَّجُلَ الصَّالِحَ عَلَى السَّيِّئَةِ الصَّغِيرَةِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ لَهُ حَسَنَاتٌ أَمْثَالُ الْجِبَالِ بِلَا سَبَبٍ أَصْلًا بَلْ بِمَحْضِ الْمَشِيئَةِ. وَأَصْلُ الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ أَنَّ الْقَادِرَ الْمُخْتَارَ يُرَجِّحُ أَحَدَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ عَلَى الْآخَرِ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ إلَى آخِرِ مَا نَقَلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -
 ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 وَبِهَذَا يَظْهَرُ الْقَوْلُ الثَّالِثُ فِي هَذَا الْأَصْلِ وَهُوَ: أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ كُلُّ مَنْ اجْتَهَدَ وَاسْتَدَلَّ يَتَمَكَّنُ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِّ وَلَا يَسْتَحِقُّ الْوَعِيدَ إلَّا مَنْ تَرَكَ مَأْمُورًا أَوْ فَعَلَ مَحْظُورًا وَهَذَا هُوَ قَوْلُ الْفُقَهَاءِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ وَهُوَ الْقَوْلُ الْمَعْرُوفُ عَنْ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَقَوْلِ جُمْهُورِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ يَجْمَعُ الصَّوَابَ مِنْ الْقَوْلَيْنِ.
translated_text:
and therefore everyone who fails to know it is punished; and the position of the Jahmiyyah Jabriyyah, who say that the servant has no power over anything whatsoever. Rather, Allah punishes solely by His will: He punishes someone who has never committed any sin and grants bliss to someone who has disbelieved and transgressed. Many later scholars have agreed with them on this.

“They say that Allah may punish children and the insane, even though they have never committed any sin. Some of them assert categorically that the children of unbelievers will be punished in the Hereafter, while others regard this as possible and say, ‘I do not know what will happen.’ They also regard it as possible that the most sinful of those who face the qiblah in prayer may be forgiven without any cause whatsoever, while a righteous man may be punished for a minor sin, even though his good deeds are like mountains—without any cause whatsoever, but solely by Allah’s will. The underlying principle shared by both groups is that an agent endowed with power and choice gives preference to one of two identical alternatives over the other without any determining factor.” And so on, to the end of what he quoted—may Allah have mercy on him.

He then said:

“This makes clear the third position on this fundamental question: not everyone who exercises independent judgment and reasons from evidence is able to know the truth, and only someone who fails to do what is commanded or does what is forbidden deserves the threatened punishment. This is the position of the jurists and imams, the position known to have been held by the early generations of the Muslim community, and the position of the majority of Muslims. It combines what is correct in the two positions.”

original_text:
فَالصَّوَابُ مِنْ الْقَوْلِ الْأَوَّلِ قَوْلُ الْجَهْمِيَّة الَّذِي وَافَقُوا فِيهِ السَّلَفَ وَالْجُمْهُورَ وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ كُلُّ مَنْ طَلَبَ وَاجْتَهَدَ وَاسْتَدَلَّ يَتَمَكَّنُ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِّ فِيهِ بَلْ اسْتِطَاعَةُ النَّاسِ فِي ذَلِكَ مُتَفَاوِتَةٌ.
وَالْقَدَرِيَّةُ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى سَوَّى بَيْنَ الْمُكَلَّفِينَ فِي الْقُدْرَةِ وَلَمْ يَخُصَّ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِمَا فَضَّلَهُمْ بِهِ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ حَتَّى آمَنُوا وَلَا خَصَّ الْمُطِيعِينَ بِمَا فَضَّلَهُمْ بِهِ عَلَى الْعُصَاةِ حَتَّى أَطَاعُوا. وَهَذَا مِنْ أَقْوَالِ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ الَّتِي خَالَفُوا بِهَا الْكِتَابَ وَالسُّنَّةَ وَإِجْمَاعَ السَّلَفِ وَالْعَقْلَ الصَّرِيحَ كَمَا بُسِطَ فِي مَوْضِعِهِ.
 وَلِهَذَا قَالُوا:
 إنَّ كُلَّ مُسْتَدِلٍّ فَمَعَهُ قُدْرَةٌ تَامَّةٌ يَتَوَصَّلُ بِهَا إلَى مَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِّ وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ النَّاسَ إذَا اشْتَبَهَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ الْقِبْلَةُ فِي السَّفَرِ فَكُلُّهُمْ مَأْمُورُونَ بِالِاجْتِهَادِ وَالِاسْتِدْلَالِ عَلَى جِهَةِ الْقِبْلَةِ ثُمَّ بَعْضُهُمْ يَتَمَكَّنُ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ جِهَتِهَا وَبَعْضُهُمْ يَعْجَزُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ فَيَغْلَطُ فَيَظُنُّ فِي بَعْضِ الْجِهَاتِ أَنَّهَا جِهَتُهَا وَلَا يَكُونُ مُصِيبًا فِي ذَلِكَ. لَكِنْ هُوَ مُطِيعٌ لِلَّهِ وَلَا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ فِي صِلَاتِهِ إلَيْهَا؛ لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى لَا يُكَلِّفُ نَفْسًا إلَّا وُسْعَهَا فَعَجْزُهُمْ عَنْ الْعِلْمِ بِهَا كَعَجْزِهِ عَنْ التَّوَجُّهِ إلَيْهَا كَالْمُقَيَّدِ وَالْخَائِفِ؛ وَالْمَحْبُوسِ وَالْمَرِيضِ الَّذِي لَا يُمْكِنُهُ التَّوَجُّهُ إلَيْهَا.
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الصَّوَابُ فِي الْأَصْلِ الثَّانِي قَوْلَ مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُعَذِّبُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ إلَّا مَنْ عَصَاهُ بِتَرْكِ
translated_text:
Thus, what is correct in the first position, that of the Jahmiyyah, is the point on which they agreed with the early generations and the majority: not everyone who seeks the truth, exercises independent judgment, and reasons from evidence is able to know the truth in the matter. Rather, people’s capacities in this regard vary.

The Qadariyyah say that Allah Most High has given all those accountable before Him equal capacity. He has not singled out the believers for anything that gave them an advantage over the unbelievers and enabled them to believe, nor singled out the obedient for anything that gave them an advantage over the disobedient and enabled them to obey. This is among the views of the Qadariyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and others in which they have contradicted the Quran, the Sunnah, the consensus of the early generations, and sound reason, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

For this reason, they say that everyone who reasons from evidence possesses the full capacity needed to attain knowledge of the truth. Yet it is well known that when people are uncertain of the direction of the qiblah while travelling, they are all commanded to exercise their judgment and use the available evidence to determine its direction. These people then argue against the Muʿtazilah, denying that reason establishes obligations and prohibitions, by citing the words of Allah Most High:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

Yet this is also evidence against them, ruling out punishment altogether before messengers have been sent, whereas they hold that punishment before the sending of messengers is possible. The former say that He punishes someone to whom He has sent no messenger because that person has committed acts whose evil is known through reason. The latter say that He even punishes those who have never done anything evil, such as children.

This contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, and reason as well. Allah Most High says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

And Allah Most High says of the people of the Fire:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’”

“They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error.”’”

Thus, He—glorified and exalted be He—has stated in universally inclusive terms that whenever a group is cast into the Fire, its keepers ask whether a warner came to them, and they acknowledge that a warner did indeed come to them. Hence, no group enters the Fire without a warner having come to them. Whoever has received no warner will therefore not enter the Fire.

And He says:

“That is because your Lord would not destroy towns unjustly while their people were unaware.”

That is, this is for this reason. Thus, it is known that He does not punish someone who is unaware unless there has come to him

a warner. This also indicates that such punishment is an injustice from which He—glorified be He—is far exalted.

Moreover, Allah Most High has stated in several places that He does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, as in His words:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

And His words:

“As for those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

And His words:

“No soul is burdened beyond its capacity.”

And His words:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it.”

He commanded people to fear Him to the best of their ability, saying:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

The believers supplicated to Him, saying:

“Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear.”

He replied:

“I have granted this.”

These texts thus indicate that He does not require any soul to do what it is incapable of doing, contrary to the determinist Jahmiyyah. They also indicate that He does not hold accountable those who err or forget, contrary to the Qadariyyah and the Muʿtazilah. This is the decisive word on this matter.

Thus, whoever strives to reach a judgment by examining the evidence—whether a leader, judge, scholar, one engaged in inquiry, mufti, or anyone else—if he exerts himself and examines the evidence, fearing Allah to the best of his ability, then this is precisely what Allah has required of him. of reward if he fears Him to the best of his ability. Allah will not punish him at all, contrary to the determinist Jahmiyyah. He is correct in the sense that he is obedient to Allah, though he may or may not know the actual truth. This is contrary to the Qadariyyah and the Muʿtazilah, who say that everyone who exerts his utmost comes to know the truth. This is false, as explained above. Rather, everyone who exerts his utmost deserves reward.

The same applies to unbelievers: if someone in a land of unbelief receives the call of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and knows that he is Allah’s Messenger, believes in him and in what was revealed to him, and fears Allah to the best of his ability, as al-Najāshī and others did, yet cannot emigrate to the land of Islam or observe all the ordinances of Islam—because he is prevented from emigrating and openly practising his religion, and has no one to teach him all the ordinances of Islam—then he is a believer and one of the people of Paradise.

Such was the believing man from Pharaoh’s household among Pharaoh’s people, and such was Pharaoh’s wife. Indeed, such was Joseph, the man of truth—peace be upon him—among the people of Egypt. They were unbelievers, and he could not put into practice among them everything he knew of the religion of Islam. He called them to worship Allah alone and to believe, but they did not respond to him. Allah Most High relates the words of the believing man from Pharaoh’s household:

“Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until, when he died, you said, ‘Allah will never send a messenger after him.’”

Likewise, although al-Najāshī was king of the Christians, his people did not obey him in

embracing Islam; rather, only a few of them embraced it with him. For this reason,

“When he died, there was no one there to offer the funeral prayer for him, so the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—offered it for him in Medina. He took the Muslims out to the prayer ground, arranged them in rows, and offered the funeral prayer for him. He informed them of his death on the very day he died, saying, ‘A righteous brother of yours from among the people of Abyssinia has died.’”

He had not observed many, or even most, of the ordinances of Islam because he was unable to do so. He did not emigrate, take part in jihad, or perform the pilgrimage to the House. Indeed, it has been reported that he did not perform the five daily prayers, fast the month of Ramadan, or pay the prescribed zakat, because these practices would have become apparent to his people, who would have objected, and he was unable to oppose them.

We know with certainty that he could not judge among them according to the Quran. Yet Allah had enjoined His Prophet in Medina, whenever the People of the Book came to him, to judge among them only according to what Allah had revealed to him. He also warned him against their luring him away from any part of what Allah had revealed to him. This includes imposing the prescribed penalty of stoning for unlawful sexual intercourse on a person of the requisite marital status, judging fairly in matters of blood money, and treating the highborn and the lowly equally in matters of bloodshed: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, and so forth.

Al-Najāshī could not judge according to the Quran, for his people would not allow him to do so. Often a man assumes office as a judge—or even a ruler—among the Muslims and the Tatars, wishing to implement certain measures of justice, but is unable to do so because others prevent him. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

And ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz faced hostility and harm because of some of the justice he established; it has even been said that he was poisoned for that reason. Al-Najāshī and others like him will enjoy bliss in Paradise, even though they did not observe those ordinances of Islam that were beyond their ability. Rather, they judged according to such laws as they were able to apply.

This is why Allah counted these people among the People of the Book. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah, in what has been revealed to you, and in what was revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah. They do not exchange Allah’s revelations for a small price. They will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.”

A group of the early generations said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Najāshī. This is reported from Jābir, Ibn ‘Abbās, and Anas. Others said that it concerned him and his companions, as al-Hasan and Qatādah stated. This is also what the Companions meant, though he was the one whom the others obeyed, for the wording of the verse is plural; it was not intended to refer to just one person.

It is reported that ‘Atā’ said: “It was revealed concerning forty people from Najrān, thirty from Abyssinia, and eight from among the Byzantines. They followed the religion of Jesus, then believed in Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

These commentators did not mention those who believed in the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in Medina, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām and others who had been Jews, or Salmān al-Fārisī and others who had been Christians. These people, however, had become numbered among the believers, so it is not said of them:

“Indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you

and in what was revealed to them.” Nor does anyone say that Jews and Christians, after embracing Islam, emigrating, and joining the ranks of the Muslims who emigrated and strove in Allah’s cause, are described as belonging to the People of the Book—that is, as still numbered among them despite having believed in the Messenger. As Allah Most High says concerning someone killed by mistake:

“Hostile to you, while he is a believer, then a believing slave must be freed.”

And His words:

“And if he belongs to a people with whom you have a treaty.”

Thus, he belongs to the enemy people, but he had believed and was unable to emigrate, openly profess his faith, or observe its ordinances. Allah therefore called him a believer because he had fulfilled as much of faith as he could.

Likewise, there was a group of believers in Mecca who concealed their faith and were unable to emigrate. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, when the angels take the souls of those who have wronged themselves, they ask, ‘What condition were you in?’ They reply, ‘We were oppressed in the land.’ The angels say, ‘Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?’ Their refuge will be Hell—what an evil destination!

Thus He, glorified be He, excused those who were helpless and unable to emigrate.

Allah Most High also says:

“And why do you not fight in the cause of Allah and for the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, ‘Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper’?”

among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange Allah’s verses for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.”

First, Ibn Salām embraced Islam as soon as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, arrived in Medina. He said: “When I saw his face, I knew that his was not the face of a liar.” The passage concerning the People of the Book in Surah Āl ʿImrān, however, was only revealed when the delegation from Najrān arrived in the year 9 or 10 AH.

Second, Ibn Salām and others like him belong to the ranks of the Companions and believers, and he is among the best of them. The same applies to Salmān al-Fārisī: he is not described as belonging to the People of the Book.

These people have rewards like those of the other believers; indeed, they are given their reward twice over. They observe all the ordinances of Islam, so their reward is greater than is conveyed by saying:

“Those will have their reward with their Lord.”

Moreover, their circumstances were plain and well known, and no one had any doubts about them. What benefit, then, would there be in making such a statement about them?

This would be no different from saying: “People who were polytheists or belonged to the People of the Book have entered Islam.” Everyone knows this, since Islam is a religion that was not known before Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Thus, everyone who entered it had previously been either a polytheist or one of the People of the Book—either a person of the Book or

a gentile. What benefit, then, is there in stating this? The case of al-Najāshī and his companions was different: they outwardly adhered to many Christian practices, so their situation could be unclear.

For this reason, accounts of the occasion of this verse’s revelation mention that when al-Najāshī died, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, offered the funeral prayer for him. Someone said: “Are you praying for this Christian foreigner while he is in his own land?” This verse was then revealed. This is reported from Jābir, Anas ibn Mālik, and Ibn ʿAbbās, who were among the Companions who participated in the funeral prayer for al-Najāshī. This differs from the case of Ibn Salām and Salmān al-Fārisī: had the Prophet offered the funeral prayer for either of them, no one would have objected.

This helps show that among those who outwardly profess Islam are hypocrites for whom the funeral prayer must not be offered, as was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy and others like him. Conversely, someone living in a land of disbelief may be a believer for whom the funeral prayer is offered, as in the case of al-Najāshī.

A similar passage occurs when Allah Most High mentions the People of the Book, saying:

“If the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.”

“They will cause you no more than annoyance. If they fight you, they will turn their backs and flee; then they will receive no help.”

“Humiliation has been laid upon them wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from people. They have incurred Allah’s anger, and destitution has been laid upon them. That is because they used to reject Allah’s signs and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and continually transgressed.”

“They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite Allah’s verses during the night and prostrate themselves.”

“They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to do good deeds. They are among the righteous.”

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions. It has also been said that His words, “Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient,” refer to ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions. This interpretation, and Allah knows best, is of the same kind as the preceding one: these men no longer belonged to the People of the Book. Rather, what is meant is someone who outwardly belongs to them and yet is a believer, but cannot do what the believers who emigrate and fight in Allah’s cause are able to do. Such was the believer from Pharaoh’s household: he belonged to Pharaoh’s household, yet he was a believer. Hence Allah Most High said:

“A believing man from Pharaoh’s household, who concealed his faith, said, ‘Would you kill a man merely for saying, “My Lord is Allah,” when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord?’”

He belonged to Pharaoh’s household, yet he was a believer. Likewise, among these people there are believers. Hence He said:

“But most of them are defiantly disobedient.”

Before this, He had said:

“If the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.”

Then He said:

“They will cause you no more than annoyance.”

This refers to all of them, not merely to the majority of them. Hence He said:

“If they fight you, they will turn their backs and flee; then they will receive no help.”

They may fight while among them is a believer who conceals his faith, joins them on the battlefield, is unable to emigrate, is compelled to fight, and will be resurrected

“An army will march against this House, and while they are in an open tract of land, the earth will swallow them up.” He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what about those among them who were compelled?” He replied, “They will be resurrected according to their intentions.”

This concerns his outward status. Even if he is killed and subjected to the rulings applicable to disbelievers, Allah will resurrect him according to his intention. Likewise, the hypocrites among us are outwardly subject to the rulings of Islam, yet they will be resurrected according to their intentions. Recompense on the Day of Resurrection is based on what is in people’s hearts, not merely on outward appearances. Hence it is narrated that al-‘Abbās said, “O Messenger of Allah, I was compelled.” He replied, “Outwardly, you were against us; as for what was in your heart, that is left to Allah.”

In short, there is no disagreement among Muslims that someone who has embraced faith while living in a land of disbelief and is unable to emigrate is not required to fulfil religious obligations beyond his ability. Rather, obligation is proportionate to ability. The same applies to matters whose rulings he does not know. If he did not know that prayer was obligatory for him and went for some time without praying, he is not required to make up those prayers according to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and the Zāhirīs, and one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school. The same applies to all other obligations, such as fasting the month of Ramadan, paying zakat, and so forth. translated_text:
they differed over making up the prayers.

Likewise, if someone engaged in transactions involving usury or gambling that he believed permissible, then learned of their prohibition after taking possession of the proceeds, should he annul the contract or not, just as we would not annul it if he had done this before embracing Islam?

Similarly, suppose he contracted a marriage that he believed valid according to their customs, but when the laws of Islam reached him, he realized that he had failed to fulfil some of its conditions—for example, he had married a woman during her waiting period, which has since expired. Is this marriage invalid, or is he allowed to remain in it, as he would if he had contracted it before embracing Islam and then become Muslim?

Underlying all of this is the question: Are revealed rulings binding upon those who do not know them, or do they become binding only after one learns of them? Or should a distinction be drawn between abrogating rulings and rulings introduced for the first time?

There are three opinions on this, corresponding to three positions within Ahmad’s school. Judge Abū Yaʿlā mentioned the two positions that make no such distinction in one of his books. He and others also mentioned, in their discussions of the principles of jurisprudence, the position that distinguishes between the two: abrogation does not take effect for a legally accountable person until the abrogating ruling reaches him. Abū al-Khattāb also derived a position holding that it does take effect before then.

Another instance is someone who omitted the required purification without knowing that it was obligatory, or prayed in a prohibited place before learning of the prohibition: must he repeat the prayer? There are two explicitly transmitted reports from Ahmad on this.

The correct position throughout this entire matter is that a ruling becomes binding only when one is able to learn of it, and that one need not make up what one did not know was obligatory. For it is established in an authentic report that

translated_text:
some of the Companions ate after dawn in Ramadan until they could distinguish the white thread from the black thread, yet the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not command them to make up their fasts. Some of them would remain in a state of major ritual impurity for a time without praying, not knowing that they could pray after performing dry ablution. This happened to Abū Dharr, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, and ʿAmmār when in that state, yet the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not command any of them to make up the missed prayers. Undoubtedly, many Muslims in Mecca and the desert regions continued praying towards Jerusalem until news of the abrogation reached them, and they were not commanded to repeat their prayers. There are many such examples.

This accords with the principle upheld by the early generations and the majority of scholars: Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. Obligation is therefore conditional upon ability, and punishment is incurred only for neglecting a duty or committing a forbidden act after the proof has been established.

May Allah bless Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—also said:

Section

In common usage, the terms “religious sciences” and “rational sciences” may stand in a relationship of broader and narrower scope, or they may denote two parallel categories. In some contexts, the correct distinction is between sciences based on transmitted revelation and those based on reason.

This is because “religious sciences” may mean what the Lawgiver has commanded, what the Lawgiver has communicated, what He has prescribed should be known, or what He has taught.

The first is knowledge prescribed by the revealed law—just as we speak of action prescribed by the revealed law. This includes what is obligatory or recommended, and may also include what is permissible under the revealed law.

The second is knowledge derived from the Lawgiver: what the Messenger taught his community through the faith, the Quran, the Book, and wisdom with which he was sent. It is what is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, or their derivative sources.

The first designation thus relates knowledge to its ruling under the revealed law, while the second relates it to

the way it is acquired and the evidence on which it rests. Thus, in the first sense, we speak of “knowledge prescribed by the revealed law,” just as we speak of “action prescribed by the revealed law.” The second usage is analogous to speaking of “rational knowledge” and “knowledge based on transmitted revelation.” In the first case, knowledge is considered in terms of praise and blame, reward and punishment, and command and prohibition: this belongs to prescriptive discourse. In the second, it is considered in terms of how it is acquired, its evidence, its soundness or unsoundness, and its correspondence or lack of correspondence to reality: this belongs to informative discourse.

Each of these two categories is, in turn, divided into two. Once it is understood that what is termed religious may be either what the Lawgiver has communicated or what He has commanded, then, regarding what He has communicated, He may either explain a rational proof for it or mention none. What He has commanded may either be intended by the Lawgiver in its own right or be necessary for His intended purpose—that without which His obligatory or recommended purpose cannot be achieved. These, then, are four categories.

If you wish, you may also divide what is commanded into what is known through reason alone and what is also known through revelation; it is then religious in respect of both communication and command.

For “known through revelation” must mean either that the Lawgiver has communicated it or that He has pointed to evidence for it. When it means what the Lawgiver has pointed to—as when He points to the signs of divine lordship, the evidence for messengership, and the like—then something can be both religious and rational. For when the Lawgiver drew people’s minds to the signs, proofs, and lessons, their minds were guided and came to know what He had guided them to.

translated_text:
Know that the Lawgiver has indicated the rational proofs for most of the major questions concerning the foundations of religion: acknowledging the Creator’s existence, His oneness, knowledge, power, will, and greatness; acknowledging reward and the messengership of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and other matters knowable through reason.

These principles, which the speculative theologians call rational matters because they are known through reason, are also known through revelation. I do not mean merely through what the Lawgiver communicates, for that yields knowledge only after the truthfulness of the one communicating it has been established. Knowledge of these matters through this means therefore depends on the rationally established acknowledgment of divine lordship and messengership. Rather, I mean through His indications and guidance, just as students acquire knowledge through teachers’ explanations and authors’ writings because of the evidence they have made clear to their minds.

This is a point that must be carefully understood. Many who fall into error—whether speculative theologians, hadith scholars, jurists, laypeople, or others—suppose that knowledge derived from revelation comes solely from accepting what the Lawgiver communicates as true. That is not so. Rather, through its indications, its drawing attention to evidence, and its guidance, revelation provides all religious knowledge that can be acquired in this way.

The second category of what is known through revelation is that which is known through the Lawgiver’s communication. This must be either something that can also be known through reason or something that cannot. If it cannot, then it is known solely through the Lawgiver’s communication. If it can also be known through reason, does such a case actually exist? That is, could there be something which the Lawgiver has communicated and which can also be known through reason, yet for which He has not indicated any rational proof? translated_text:
to which they had not found their way, while omitting the specious arguments and falsehoods into which they have fallen, numerous and inconsistent as these are. I have explained this general point in detail elsewhere.

If, however, “revealed knowledge” means knowledge whose acquisition is prescribed by revelation, this includes all knowledge that is recommended or obligatory, and may also include permissible knowledge. On this understanding, the foundations of religion also belong to revealed knowledge. Even what is known through reason alone belongs to revealed knowledge if revelation commands that it be known.

Accordingly, revealed knowledge falls into two categories: rational and transmitted. Here, “transmitted” replaces “revealed” as used in the first classification. It is thus clear that any rational knowledge which revelation commands us to acquire, or for which it provides evidence, is also revealed knowledge—whether by virtue of that command, that evidence, or both.

This clarification shows that rational knowledge falling outside the category of revealed knowledge—that which the Lawgiver neither commands us to acquire nor provides evidence for—is on a par with crafts such as farming, building, and weaving. This applies only to branches of knowledge of lesser merit and inferior rank. It also becomes clear that the category of revealed knowledge is nobler and broader, and that rational and revealed knowledge overlap in scope: neither constitutes a mutually exclusive alternative to the other. Rather, transmitted knowledge is the counterpart of rational knowledge. A body of knowledge can thus be rational while also being revealed in all three respects: the Lawgiver has communicated it, commanded its acquisition, and provided evidence for it. Reflect, then, that attribution

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām also said:

A Comprehensive and Beneficial Section

The terms to which Allah has attached rulings in the Quran and Sunnah include the following:

Some have definitions and meanings known through revealed Law, as Allah and His Messenger have explained them. Examples include prayer, zakat, fasting, Hajj, faith, Islam, disbelief, and hypocrisy.

Others are defined by the language itself, such as the sun and moon, heaven and earth, and land and sea.

Still others are defined by people’s customary practices and usage, and thus vary with their customs. Examples include sale, marriage, taking possession, the dirham, the dinar, and similar terms for which the Lawgiver has prescribed no definition, nor is there a single definition shared by all speakers of the language. Rather, their measure and characteristics differ according to people’s customs.

Allah and His Messenger have explained whatever belongs to the first category. As for the second and third categories, the Companions and Successors addressed by the Quran and Sunnah understood what was intended, because they knew what these terms denoted, whether delimited by the language or left to people’s customary usage

translated_text:
and practice, without any definition prescribed by revealed Law or fixed by language. This is how a sound understanding of the Quran and Sunnah is attained.

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, defines what a term denotes, this does not necessarily mean that he has departed from its linguistic meaning or broadened it. Rather, the point is that his intended meaning is known through his own explanation, peace and blessings be upon him, whatever the case may be; this is what matters. An example is the term khamr (wine): he explained that every intoxicant is khamr, thereby making clear what is meant by it in the Quran. Whether the Arabs had previously applied the word khamr to every intoxicant or restricted it to grape juice need not be determined. What is required is to know what Allah and His Messenger intended by this term. This is known through the Messenger’s explanation, peace and blessings be upon him, and through the fact that, in the language of those addressed by the Quran, khamr included date wine and other varieties. In Medina, they had no wine other than these.

Since this is so, no one may restrict the scope of terms that Allah has left unrestricted and to which He has attached rulings—commands, prohibitions, and declarations of lawfulness or unlawfulness—except on the basis of evidence from Allah and His Messenger.

One example is the term water, which is unrestricted in the Quran and Sunnah. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not divide it into two categories: water that purifies and water that does not. Such a division therefore contradicts the Quran and Sunnah. Allah simply said:

“and find no water”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that anything properly called water is pure and purifying, whether it has been used for obligatory or recommended purification

or for purification that is not recommended; and whether or not an impurity has fallen into it, provided that any such impurity is known to have undergone transformation and been wholly absorbed into it. If, however, traces of the impurity remain apparent in the water, using it is forbidden, because that amounts to using something forbidden.

Section

Another example is the term menstruation. Allah has attached numerous rulings to it in the Quran and Sunnah, yet neither its minimum nor its maximum duration has been specified, nor the duration of the interval of purity between two menstrual periods, despite how commonly this affects the Muslim community and their need to know its rulings. Nor does the language distinguish between one duration and another. Whoever fixes a limit in this matter has therefore contradicted the Quran and Sunnah. Some scholars set both a maximum and a minimum duration, though they disagree over those limits.

Others set a maximum but no minimum. The third view is the most correct: there is neither a minimum nor a maximum duration. Rather, whatever bleeding a woman experiences as a consistent, recurring pattern is menstruation. Even if it lasts less than a day, if that remains her consistent pattern, it is menstruation. Likewise, if its maximum duration is seventeen days and that remains her consistent pattern, it is menstruation.

If, however, she bleeds continuously without interruption, this is known not to be menstruation. For both revealed Law and language establish that a woman is sometimes free of menstruation and sometimes menstruating, and that her state of purity has its rulings, while her menstruation has its rulings.

وَالْعَادَةُ الْغَالِبَةُ أَنَّهَا تَحِيضُ رُبُعَ الزَّمَانِ سِتَّةً أَوْ سَبْعَةً وَإِلَى ذَلِكَ رَدَّ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الْمُسْتَحَاضَةَ الَّتِي لَيْسَ لَهَا عَادَةٌ وَلَا تَمْيِيزٌ وَالطُّهْرُ بَيْنَ الْحَيْضَتَيْنِ لَا حَدَّ لِأَكْثَرِهِ بِاتِّفَاقِهِمْ. إذْ مِنْ النِّسْوَةِ مَنْ لَا تَحِيضُ بِحَالِ وَهَذِهِ إذَا تَبَاعَدَ مَا بَيْنَ أَقْرَائِهَا فَهَلْ تَعْتَدُّ بِثُلُثِ حَيْضٍ أَوْ تَكُونُ كَالْمُرْتَابَةِ تَحِيضُ سَنَةً؟ فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ لِلْفُقَهَاءِ. وَكَذَلِكَ أَقَلُّهُ عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ لَا حَدَّ لَهُ بَلْ قَدْ تَحِيضُ الْمَرْأَةُ فِي الشَّهْرِ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ وَإِنْ قُدِّرَ أَنَّهَا حَاضَتْ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ فِي أَقَلَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَمْكَنُ لَكِنْ إذَا ادَّعَتْ انْقِضَاءَ عِدَّتِهَا فِيمَا يُخَالِفُ الْعَادَةَ الْمَعْرُوفَةَ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَشْهَدَ لَهَا بِطَانَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا كَمَا رُوِيَ عَنْ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ فِيمَنْ ادَّعَتْ ثَلَاثَ حِيَضٍ فِي شَهْرٍ. وَالْأَصْلُ فِي كُلِّ مَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْ الرَّحِمِ أَنَّهُ حَيْضٌ حَتَّى يَقُومَ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّهُ اسْتِحَاضَةٌ؛ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الدَّمُ الْأَصْلِيُّ الْجَبَلِيُّ وَهُوَ دَمٌ تُرْخِيه الرَّحِمُ وَدَمُ الْفَسَادِ دَمُ عِرْقٍ يَنْفَجِرُ؛ وَذَلِكَ كَالْمَرَضِ؛ وَالْأَصْلُ الصِّحَّةُ لَا الْمَرَضُ. فَمَتَى رَأَتْ الْمَرْأَةُ الدَّمَ جَارٍ مِنْ رَحِمِهَا فَهُوَ حَيْضٌ تُتْرَكُ لِأَجْلِهِ الصَّلَاةُ.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّهَا تَغْتَسِلُ عَقِيبَ يَوْمٍ وَلَيْلَةٍ فَهُوَ قَوْلٌ مُخَالِفٌ لِلْمَعْلُومِ مِنْ السُّنَّةِ وَإِجْمَاعِ السَّلَفِ؛ فَإِنَّا نَعْلَمُ أَنَّ النِّسَاءَ كُنَّ يَحِضْنَ عَلَى عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَكُلُّ امْرَأَةٍ تَكُونُ فِي أَوَّلِ أَمْرِهَا مُبْتَدَأَةً قَدْ ابْتَدَأَهَا الْحَيْضُ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَلَمْ يَأْمُرْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
The usual pattern is for a woman to menstruate for a quarter of the time—six or seven days. This is the pattern to which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, directed a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding who had neither an established cycle nor a way to distinguish menstrual from non-menstrual blood.

The scholars agree that there is no maximum duration for the interval of purity between two menstrual periods, since some women do not menstruate at all. If a woman has lengthy intervals between her menstrual periods, does she calculate her waiting period by one-third of a menstrual period, or is she treated like a woman whose condition is uncertain, menstruating for a year? The jurists hold two views on this.

Likewise, according to the correct view, there is no minimum duration for the interval of purity. A woman may have three menstrual periods in a month; even three periods in less time than that are possible. However, if she claims that her waiting period has ended within a duration contrary to the usual known pattern, members of her family familiar with her condition must testify on her behalf. This accords with what is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning a woman who claimed to have had three menstrual periods in one month.

The basic presumption is that everything discharged from the womb is menstruation unless evidence establishes that it is non-menstrual bleeding. Menstrual blood is the normal, natural blood released by the womb, whereas abnormal bleeding comes from a ruptured vein. The latter is like illness, whereas the presumption is health, not illness. Thus, whenever a woman sees blood flowing from her womb, it is menstruation, on account of which she refrains from prayer.

The view that she should take a ritual bath after one day and one night contradicts what is known from the Sunnah and the consensus of the early generations. We know that women menstruated during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and every woman initially experiences menstruation for the first time. Yet despite this, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not instruct
