any of them to take a ritual bath after one day and one night. Had such an instruction been transmitted, it would have established a minimum duration for menstruation. Yet the hadith scholars agree that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, set no minimum duration for it. The reports transmitted on this matter specify three days, but the scholars versed in his hadith agree that these reports are falsely attributed to him. This is the view of the vast majority of scholars and one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school.

Likewise, if a woman’s established menstrual pattern changes—whether her period becomes longer or shorter, or shifts in timing—the bleeding is menstruation until its persistence establishes that it is non-menstrual bleeding. Her case is like that of a woman menstruating for the first time.

A woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding should refer first to her established cycle, then to her ability to distinguish between the types of blood, and then to the usual menstrual pattern among women. A Sunnah ruling has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for each of these three cases. Imam Ahmad adopted all three Sunnah rulings. Some scholars adopted two of the hadiths, while others adopted only one, according to what had reached them and the conclusions of their independent reasoning. May Allah be pleased with them all.

If a pregnant woman sees blood following her familiar pattern, it is menstrual blood, in accordance with the basic presumption.

translated_text:
blood for more than forty, sixty, or seventy days and it then stopped, it would be postpartum bleeding. If, however, it continued without interruption, it would be abnormal bleeding. In that case, the limit is forty days, since this is the upper end of the usual duration, as indicated by the transmitted reports. Nor is there an age limit beyond which a woman cannot menstruate. If, after sixty or seventy years of age, her familiar uterine bleeding increased, it would be menstruation.

The loss of expectation mentioned in His words,

“And those who no longer expect menstruation,”

does not mean reaching a particular age. [For] (1) if it meant reaching a particular age, Allah and His Messenger would have specified it. Rather, it means that the woman herself no longer expects to menstruate. If her bleeding stops and she no longer expects it to return, she has ceased to expect menstruation, even if she is forty years old. If she then waits and the bleeding returns, it becomes clear that she had not ceased menstruating permanently. If it returns after the three months, her case is like that of other women whose menstruation returns after they had ceased to expect it, or whose menstrual status is uncertain.

Anyone who does not understand this cessation of expectation in this way adopts an inconsistent position if he defines it by age. His position is likewise inconsistent if he defines it neither by age nor by the woman’s loss of hope that she will menstruate. Nor can it be known simply from the person herself.

Since postpartum bleeding has no fixed duration, whether a woman gives birth to twins or more, she remains in the state of postpartum bleeding as long as she continues to see blood. Whatever blood she sees from the onset of labour is postpartum bleeding. The rulings governing postpartum bleeding are the same as those governing menstrual bleeding.

Anyone who does not adopt this view, but instead sets the minimum duration of menstruation at one day, one day and one night, or three days, has no reliable basis for doing so. For the reports on this matter transmitted from

If someone knows only of menstruation lasting three days, another says that he knows of it lasting a day and a night. If someone knows only of it lasting a day and a night, another knows of it lasting a day. We cannot deny what we do not know. If we make what we know the limit prescribed by religious law, saying, “There is no menstruation lasting less than three days, a day and a night, or a day,” merely because that is all we know, we would be devising religious law ourselves on the basis of that knowledge. If this were truly a limit prescribed by religious law, the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) would have been better placed than us to know and explain it, just as he specified for the community the limits Allah had prescribed for them: the times of prayer, Hajj, and fasting; the designated places for Hajj; the minimum thresholds and prescribed dues of zakat; and the number of prayers and their bowings and prostrations. Had Allah and His Messenger prescribed a limit for menstruation, or for anything else whose limits the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) did not specify, the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) would have explained it. His not specifying a limit therefore indicates that he left the matter to what women recognize and what is called menstruation in ordinary language.

For this reason, when asked about menstruation, many of the early generations would say, “Ask the women, for they know more about it.” That is, they know what does and does not occur in menstruation. The religious ruling is attached to the term that denotes the actual occurrence. Thus, any bleeding that occurs is menstruation unless it is known to be blood from a vein or a wound. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded his community to wipe over leather socks. Safwān ibn ‘Assāl said:

“The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded us, when we were on a journey—or travelling—not to remove our leather socks for three days and nights, except because of major ritual impurity, but not because of defecation, urination or sleep.”

He did not qualify this according to whether the leather sock stays in place on its own or not, or whether it is free of holes and splits or not. Whatever is called a leather sock and is worn and walked in may be wiped over in the manner permitted by Allah and His Messenger. Anything equivalent to it may likewise be wiped over. Being called a leather sock is not itself a determining factor; rather, the ruling concerns what is worn and walked in. Hence wiping over socks is mentioned in the hadith.

Section

Allah and His Messenger made shortening the prayers and breaking the fast conditional upon what is called travel, without specifying a distance or distinguishing between long and short journeys. Had travel been defined by a particular distance, Allah and His Messenger would have explained it. Nor does the language assign it a fixed distance. Thus, whatever speakers of the language call travel permits shortening the prayers and breaking the fast, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. The people of Mecca shortened their prayers with the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) on their journey to ‘Arafāt, which is one barīd (a postal stage) from Mecca. This shows that setting a limit of one, two or three days is not a universally applicable limit prescribed by Islamic law.

What has been reported from the Companions concerning this may relate to particular circumstances in which travel would necessarily have been of that extent. This explains why differing reports have been transmitted from individual Companions, such as Ibn ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Abbās and others. It is therefore clear that they did not establish a universally applicable legal limit for the traveller or the duration, comparable to the prescribed times for fasting and prayer. Rather, they specified it for particular people according to what they considered travel for someone in those circumstances—just as one defines deviation on the part of the rich and the poor in particular cases according to one’s judgment.

This is not because Islamic law has assigned a single amount of wealth by which everyone alike is classified as rich or poor. Rather, a little may suffice for one man, while many times that amount may not suffice for another because of his many dependants and needs; and the reverse may also be true.

Some people may cover a great distance without being travellers, such as a courier

Travel, then, is a particular form of going from place to place; it is not defined by distance or duration. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would go to Qubā’ every Saturday, sometimes riding and sometimes walking, without being a traveller. When the people of Mecca went out to Minā and ‘Arafah, however, they were travellers: they took provisions, spent the night outside the town, and made the preparations appropriate to travel. This differs from someone who goes out for Friday prayer or some other need and returns that same day: even if he covers a barīd, he may not be called a traveller.

translated_text:
to it is like going out to another part of the town. In a large town extending more than a barīd, someone going from one end to the other is not a traveller. People distinguish between someone moving about among dwellings and their dependencies and a traveller departing from all of them. Thus, the inhabitants of the Prophet’s city (peace and blessings be upon him) would go to their orchards without being travellers. Medina had no wall; rather, it consisted of separate tribal quarters and clusters of houses, with a considerable distance between its two sides. Someone going from one tribal quarter to another was not a traveller, even if each tribe had its orchards and fields around it, for the name Medina encompassed all of this.

Hence Allah Most High says:

“Among the Bedouins around you are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those entrenched in hypocrisy.”

People are thus divided into two groups: desert dwellers, who are the Bedouins, and the people of Medina. All those living in mud-brick dwellings were therefore people of Medina. This includes Qubā’ and other places, showing that the name Medina encompassed all of them. For it did not have a wall as it does today, with gates that are opened and closed. It merely had approaches. Even if those approaches lay inward of Qubā’ and other places, the name Medina could encompass the town’s settled area.

This is familiar in every city. Someone says, “I went to Damascus, Misr, Baghdad, or elsewhere; I lived there and stayed there for a time,” or something similar, although he was living outside the walls. The city’s name encompasses all those dwellings, even though the interior

within the walls is more specifically denoted by the name than the area outside. Likewise, the city of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) had an inner and an outer area, separated by its approaches, and the name Medina encompasses all of this in the Book of Allah Most High. Thus, all these inhabitants used to offer the Friday prayer and the two Eid prayers behind the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his successors. No separate Friday or Eid prayers were held in Qubā’ or elsewhere, whereas the five daily prayers were offered in every tribal quarter. The Prophet’s statement (peace and blessings be upon him), “There are indeed men in Medina,” is another example of this: it encompasses all the dwellings.

Likewise, the term qurā (towns) includes cities, as in His words:

“How many towns We have destroyed!”

And His words:

“So that you may warn the Mother of Towns and those around it.”

And His words:

“Your Lord would never destroy towns until He had sent a messenger to their principal town, reciting Our revelations to them. Nor would We ever destroy towns unless their people were wrongdoers.”

And His words:

“These are some of the accounts of the towns which We relate to you; some are still standing, while others have been mown down.”

This encompasses dwellings both within and outside the town, even if a wall or something similar separates them. For the sending of messengers, destruction, and the like did not apply to some inhabitants to the exclusion of others. Most cities have both an inner and an outer area.

translated_text:
The word “Kaaba” originally names the structure itself, but in the Quran it is also used to include the surrounding area, as in His words:

“An offering to be brought to the Kaaba.”

Likewise, “the Sacred Mosque” denotes both the mosque and the surrounding sanctuary. Similarly, Badr is the name of a well, but the surrounding area is also called by that name. Uhud, too, is the name of the mountain, yet it includes the surrounding area. Thus, people say, “The battle took place at Uhud,” although it actually took place below the mountain.

The same applies to places named after a mountain pass or a palace. Al-‘Uqayba is the diminutive of al-‘Aqaba (the mountain pass), and al-Qusayr is the diminutive of qasr (palace). There may originally have been a small palace or a small pass there, after which the name came to encompass the surrounding area, however extensive. This is very common in place names.

The point is that someone moving about among the dwellings is not called a traveler. If people customarily spend the night in their orchards and have dwellings there, going out to them is like going to another part of their residential area. A traveler is therefore not a traveler until he emerges, becoming exposed and visible in the open country beyond the dwellings, where the wayfarer does not travel but ordinarily becomes visible and exposed. The point is that what constitutes travel is determined by the meaning of the word in language and customary usage.

Section

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No zakat is due on less than five wasqs, less than five ūqiyyas, or fewer than five camels.”

He also said:

“No zakat is due on silver until it reaches two hundred dirhams.”

Regarding the thief, he said:

“His hand is to be cut off if he steals something worth the price of a shield.”

He also said:

“The hand is to be cut off for stealing a quarter of a dinar.”

In his usage, an ūqiyya was forty dirhams. Yet he specified no fixed measure for either the dirham or the dinar. He did not mint any dirhams himself, nor were dirhams minted in his land; rather, they were imported, already minted by unbelievers.

These included both large and small coins. People sometimes transacted with them by number and sometimes by weight, as he said:

“Weigh it out and give extra, for the best people are those who repay their debts most generously.”

There was a man there who weighed coins for a fee. Clearly, when they weighed them, they needed a standard weight by which to determine the weight of the dirhams. But the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, neither fixed nor specified this standard. It has been related that dirhams were of three kinds: eight dāniqs, six, and four. Perhaps the seller would specify one of these kinds, and the buyer would pay him according to its weight.

translated_text:
the small dirhams amounting to five ūqiyyas—two hundred dirhams—must pay zakat. The same applies to medium-sized and large dirhams. Accordingly, people follow their customary practices regarding the weights of dirhams and dinars: whatever they agree upon and designate as a dirham is a dirham, and whatever they designate as a dinar is a dinar. The Lawgiver’s words encompass what they customarily use, whether small or large. If their customary dirhams are large and they know no others, zakat is not due from a person until he possesses two hundred of them. If they are small and they know no others, zakat becomes due when he possesses two hundred of them. If they use a mixture, zakat becomes due when he possesses that number in total. This applies whether the coins are of a single issue or different issues, and whether they are pure or debased, so long as they are called dirhams without qualification. This is the view of several scholars.

If, however, a coin is called a dirham only with a qualification—for example, if it consists mostly of copper and is called a “black dirham,” falling outside the unqualified term “dirham”—then this requires further consideration. Accordingly, the correct view is that zakat is obligatory on two hundred debased dirhams, as held by Abū Hanīfa and in one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school. If a thief steals three dirhams, whether large, small, or a mixture of both, his hand is to be cut off.

Thus, when the Lawgiver made the obligation conditional upon possessing five wasqs, He tied it to a fixed quantity that was the same for everyone. This was unlike the five ūqiyyas, which did not constitute a fixed quantity common to everyone; rather, their customary amount was greater among some people than among others. This resembles the terms “mosque,” “house,” “residence,” “city,” and “village”: their customary sizes vary from one people to another, yet the Lawgiver’s wording encompasses them all.

If someone were to say that the sāʿ and the mudd should be determined by people’s customary usage, arguing that ʿUmar’s sāʿ was larger and that he used it to collect the land tax—being eight ratls, as the scholars of Iraq maintain—this could be conceivable where the inhabitants of a locality have two measures, one large and one small. The charity due at the end of Ramadan would then be measured by the larger one, and a wasq would equal sixty of those larger measures. For the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, specified both the zakat threshold for produce measured in wasqs and the amount of that charity in terms of the sāʿ; he did not specify any zakat threshold or obligatory amount in terms of the mudd.

However, I know of no one who held this view. Nor may we advance any position other than what our predecessors stated, for they certainly knew what the Messenger intended. They may therefore be told: Granted that this was so, when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, addressed his Companions and his community using the terms “dirham” and “dinar,” while they had coins of differing weights, as you have mentioned, he did not define the dirham for them by an average weight as ʿAbd al-Malik did. Rather, he used the terms “dirham” and “dinar” without qualification, just as he used the terms “shirt,” “trousers,” “waist-wrapper,” “cloak,” “residence,” “village,” “city,” “house,” and other things made by human beings. Had he intended a fixed measure for what these terms designated, he would have specified it, knowing that their sizes varied. People’s agreement upon a particular weight for the dirham and dinar is therefore a matter of custom.

The cubit is more closely connected to the natural constitution of created beings than these are. Originally, a cubit is a human forearm, and a human being is created. One forearm exceeds another in length only by a difference determined at creation, over which people have no choice. This differs from things people make by choice, such as dirhams, cities, and residences, which have no fixed measure. Rather, clothing follows people’s bodily dimensions, while residences and cities are proportioned to their needs.

As for the dirham and dinar, no fixed measure is known for them, whether by nature or religious law. Rather, their measure is determined by custom and convention. This is because, fundamentally, they are not themselves the object sought; their purpose is to serve as a standard for what people exchange. Dirhams and dinars are not sought for their own sake; rather, they are a means of conducting transactions

Section

Likewise, religious law has not specified a fixed quantity for feeding ten needy people. Rather, it is as Allah says:

“from the average food you feed your families.”

In every locality, people are to provide others with enough of the average food they themselves eat, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

The same applies to the terms “jizyah” (poll tax) and “diyah” (blood money). The former follows the pattern fi‘lah, from jazā–yajzī, meaning to discharge or pay an obligation. This is the sense of the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“It suffices for you, but it will not suffice for anyone after you.”

The underlying construction is jazā, jizyah (“he paid; payment”), just as one says wa‘ada, ‘idah (“he promised; a promise”), and wazana, zinah (“he weighed; weight”). Likewise, diyah derives from wadā–yadī–diyah (“to pay blood money; blood money”), just as one says wa‘ada–ya‘idu–‘idah (“to promise; a promise”).

A verbal noun is often used to name the object of its action. Thus, what is paid is called diyah, and what is discharged and settled is called jizyah, just as what is promised is called a “promise” in His words:

“They say, ‘When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?’ Say, ‘Knowledge is with Allah alone, and I am only a clear warner.’ Then, when they see it close at hand…”

What they see is the punishment they were promised. Similarly, such a payment is called itāwah (tribute) because it is given. The same applies to darībah (a levy), which denotes what is imposed upon people. None of these expressions has a fixed limit inherent in its linguistic meaning; rather, reference is made to people’s customs. If, however, religious law has fixed a limit for any of them, that limit must be observed.

For this reason, the jurists differed over jizyah: is its amount fixed by religious law, or is it left to the independent judgment of the rulers? The same applies to kharāj (land tax). The correct view is that their amounts are not fixed by religious law. The Prophet’s instruction to Mu‘ādh, may Allah bless the Prophet and grant him peace,

“to take from every male who had reached puberty one dinar or its equivalent in Ma‘āfirī cloth,”

was a ruling for a particular case. He did not make it a general rule applying until the Day of Resurrection to everyone from whom jizyah is collected. This is shown by the fact that he concluded an agreement with the people of Bahrain on the basis of

 هِيَ مُقَدَّرَةٌ بِالشَّرْعِ تَقْدِيرًا عَامًّا لِلْأُمَّةِ كَتَقْدِيرِ الصَّلَاةِ وَالزَّكَاةِ وَقَدْ تَخْتَلِفُ بِاخْتِلَافِ أَقْوَالِ النَّاسِ فِي جِنْسِهَا وَقَدْرِهَا وَهَذَا أَقْرَبُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ وَعَلَيْهِ تَدُلُّ الْآثَارُ وَأَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إنَّمَا جَعَلَهَا مِائَةً لِأَقْوَامٍ كَانَتْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ الْإِبِلَ؛ وَلِهَذَا جَعَلَهَا عَلَى أَهْلِ الذَّهَبِ ذَهَبًا؛ وَعَلَى أَهْلِ الْفِضَّةِ فِضَّةً؛ وَعَلَى أَهْلِ الشَّاءِ شَاءً؛ وَعَلَى أَهْلِ الثِّيَابِ ثِيَابًا؛ وَبِذَلِكَ مَضَتْ سِيرَةُ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ وَغَيْرِهِ.
فَصْلٌ:
وَقَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَالَّذِينَ هُمْ لِفُرُوجِهِمْ حَافِظُونَ}
 
{إلَّا عَلَى أَزْوَاجِهِمْ أوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ}
 وَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{احْفَظْ عَوْرَتَك إلَّا مِنْ زَوْجَتِك أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ يَمِينُك}
 وَقَدْ دَلَّ الْقُرْآنُ عَلَى أَنَّ مَا حُرِّمَ وَطْؤُهُ بِالنِّكَاحِ
translated_text:
a levy on each male who had reached puberty, without fixing it at that amount; this, too, was jizyah. Likewise, he reached an agreement with the people of Najrān for payments different from these and not fixed at that amount. This shows that the matter rests on what the ruler considers beneficial and what those entering into the treaty agree to. It then becomes an obligation upon them which they discharge—that is, they undertake and pay it.

As for diyah, in cases of intentional killing it depends on the agreement of the two parties. In cases of accidental killing, however, religious law makes it a definite obligation, so it cannot depend on their mutual agreement. Rather, it may be said that religious law has fixed it generally for the entire Muslim community, just as it has prescribed prayer and zakah. It may also vary according to people’s differing views concerning its kind and amount. This is the more plausible of the two views, and the transmitted reports support it: the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fixed it at one hundred camels only for people whose wealth consisted of camels. Accordingly, he prescribed gold for those whose wealth was in gold, silver for those whose wealth was in silver, sheep for those whose wealth was in sheep, and garments for those whose wealth was in garments. This was also the practice of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb and others.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Guard your private parts except from your wife or those your right hand possesses.”

The Quran also indicates that anyone with whom intercourse is forbidden through marriage

فَصْلٌ:
النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَضَى بِالدِّيَةِ عَلَى الْعَاقِلَةِ وَهُمْ:
 الَّذِينَ يَنْصُرُونَ الرَّجُلَ وَيُعِينُونَهُ وَكَانَتْ الْعَاقِلَةُ عَلَى عَهْدِهِ هُمْ عَصَبَتُهُ. فَلَمَّا كَانَ فِي زَمَنِ عُمَرَ جَعَلَهَا عَلَى أَهْلِ الدِّيوَانِ؛ وَلِهَذَا اخْتَلَفَ فِيهَا الْفُقَهَاءُ
translated_text:
is likewise forbidden through slave ownership. Thus, a man may not take as concubines women whom he is permanently forbidden to marry. Nor may he have intercourse with a concubine while in the pilgrim state of consecration, while fasting, during her menstruation, or in any other circumstances in which intercourse with a wife is prohibited; the prohibition applies all the more to a concubine.

As for the waiting period to establish that the womb is free of pregnancy, the Sunnah has not prescribed it unconditionally for every female slave. Rather, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade a man to water another man’s crop with his own fluid.

He also said concerning the female captives of Awtās:

“No pregnant woman is to be approached sexually until she gives birth, nor a woman who is not pregnant until she has completed the waiting period to establish that her womb is free of pregnancy.”

This concerned slaves taken as captives. He did not say the same concerning women acquired by inheritance, purchase, or other means. The requirement, then, is that if a female slave has been having intercourse, intercourse with her is forbidden until she has completed that waiting period, lest a man water another man’s crop with his own fluid.

But if it is known that her owner was not having intercourse with her—because she is a virgin, because the owner is a woman or a child, or because he truthfully states, “I was not having intercourse with her”—then neither a revealed text nor analogy provides any basis for prohibiting intercourse with her until she has completed that waiting period.

Section

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled that blood money was payable by the ʿāqilah: those who support a man and come to his aid. In his time, a man’s ʿāqilah consisted of his agnatic kin. When ʿUmar’s time came, he placed this liability upon those enrolled in the dīwān (state register). Hence the jurists differed concerning it.

original_text:
فَيُقَالُ:
 أَصْلُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ الْعَاقِلَةَ هُمْ مَحْدُودُونَ بِالشَّرْعِ أَوْ هُمْ مَنْ يَنْصُرُهُ وَيُعِينُهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَعْيِينٍ. فَمَنْ قَالَ بِالْأَوَّلِ لَمْ يَعْدِلْ عَنْ الْأَقَارِبِ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ الْعَاقِلَةُ عَلَى عَهْدِهِ. وَمَنْ قَالَ بِالثَّانِي جَعَلَ الْعَاقِلَةَ فِي كُلِّ زَمَانٍ وَمَكَانٍ مَنْ يَنْصُرُ الرَّجُلَ وَيُعِينُهُ فِي ذَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ وَالْمَكَانِ. فَلَمَّا كَانَ فِي عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إنَّمَا يَنْصُرُهُ وَيُعِينُهُ أَقَارِبُهُ كَانُوا هُمْ الْعَاقِلَةَ؛ إذْ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَى عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ دِيوَانٌ وَلَا عَطَاءٌ فَلَمَّا وَضَعَ عُمَرُ الدِّيوَانَ كَانَ مَعْلُومًا أَنَّ جُنْدَ كُلِّ مَدِينَةٍ يَنْصُرُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا وَيُعِينُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُونُوا أَقَارِبَ فَكَانُوا هُمْ الْعَاقِلَةَ. وَهَذَا أَصَحُّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ.

{قَضَى فِي الْمَرْأَةِ الْقَاتِلَةِ أَنَّ عَقْلَهَا عَلَى عَصَبَتِهَا؛ وَأَنَّ مِيرَاثَهَا لِزَوْجِهَا وَبَنِيهَا}

 كَمَا قَضَى بِهِ عُمَرُ وَيَجْعَلُ ذَلِكَ بَعْضُهُمْ إجْمَاعًا وَبَعْضُهُمْ قَالَ:
 لَا تَكُونُ إلَّا حَالَّةً. وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّ تَعْجِيلَهَا وَتَأْجِيلَهَا بِحَسَبِ الْحَالِ وَالْمَصْلَحَةِ فَإِنْ كَانُوا مَيَاسِيرَ وَلَا ضَرَرَ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي التَّعْجِيلِ أُخِذَتْ
translated_text:
and it may be said:

The fundamental question is whether the membership of the ʿāqilah is fixed by the revealed law, or whether it comprises whoever supports a person and comes to his aid, without specifying particular people. Those who adopt the first view restrict it to relatives, for they constituted the ʿāqilah in the Prophet’s time. Those who adopt the second regard a man’s ʿāqilah, in every time and place, as those who support him and come to his aid in that time and place. In the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it was a man’s relatives who supported him and came to his aid, so they constituted his ʿāqilah. There was then neither a state register nor stipends. When ʿUmar established the register, it was well known that the soldiers of each city supported and assisted one another, even if they were unrelated, so they constituted the ʿāqilah. This is the sounder of the two views: its composition varies according to circumstances.

Otherwise, consider a man who has settled in the West, where there are people who support him and come to his aid. How could his ʿāqilah consist of people in the East, in another kingdom, who may no longer even receive news of him? An inheritance, however, can be preserved for an absent heir. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“ruled concerning a woman who had killed someone that the blood money payable on her behalf was the responsibility of her agnatic kin, while her inheritance belonged to her husband and sons.”

Thus, the heirs are distinct from the ʿāqilah. The same applies to allowing a three-year term for payment of the blood money. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not defer its payment, but ruled that it was payable immediately, whereas ʿUmar allowed three years for its payment. Many jurists therefore say that payment must be deferred, as ʿUmar ruled; some even consider this a matter of consensus. Others say that it must be paid immediately.

The correct view is that immediate or deferred payment depends on the circumstances and the interests served. If those liable are well-to-do and immediate payment would cause them no harm, it is collected

فَصْلٌ:
وَقَدْ قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِي آيَةِ الْخُمُسِ:
 
{فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ وَلِلرَّسُولِ وَلِذِي الْقُرْبَى وَالْيَتَامَى وَالْمَسَاكِينِ}
 وَمِثْلُ ذَلِكَ فِي آيَةِ الْفَيْءِ.
 وَقَالَ فِي آيَةِ الصَّدَقَاتِ:
 
{لِلْفُقَرَاءِ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَالْعَامِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا}

 وَلَيْسَ فِي اللَّفْظِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّسْوِيَةِ بَلْ عَلَى خِلَافِهَا فَمَنْ أَوْجَبَ بِاللَّفْظِ التَّسْوِيَةَ فَقَدْ قَالَ مَا يُخَالِفُ الْكِتَابَ وَالسُّنَّةَ أَلَا تَرَى أَنَّ اللَّهَ لَمَّا قَالَ:

translated_text:
immediately; if doing so would cause hardship, payment is deferred.

This is Ahmad’s explicit position: deferral is not obligatory, contrary to the view of many of his followers, who deemed it obligatory, agreeing with those among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik and others who held that view. This opinion is exceedingly weak. It resembles the view that the Muslim community may abrogate the law of its Prophet, as some people maintain when they say that consensus can be abrogated. This is among the views Ahmad most strongly rejected. An established Sunnah cannot be set aside except by another established Sunnah. Nor can a consensus contrary to a Sunnah arise unless that consensus is accompanied by a known Sunnah which we know abrogates the earlier one.

Section

Allah Most High says in the verse concerning the one-fifth share of war spoils:

“One-fifth of it belongs to Allah, the Messenger, near relatives, orphans and the needy.”

The same appears in the verse concerning spoils acquired without fighting. In the verse concerning zakat, He says:

“For the poor, the needy, and those employed to administer it,”

and so on to the end of the verse. Allah thus mentions the categories without further restriction. Nothing in the wording indicates that they must receive equal shares; rather, it indicates the opposite. Whoever maintains that the wording requires equal distribution has therefore said something contrary to the Book and the Sunnah. Do you not see that, when Allah said:

“But the truly righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture and the prophets, and give wealth, despite their love for it, to relatives, orphans and the needy

and the wayfarer.” He Most High also says:

“Give near relatives their due, as well as the needy and the wayfarer.”

He Most High says:

“If relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, give them something from it.”

He Most High says:

“And those in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived.”

He Most High says:

“So eat of them and feed those who are content and those who come seeking help.”

Equal distribution was not obligatory in any of these or similar cases? Indeed, in most of these cases it is not even recommended, whether giving itself is obligatory or recommended. Rather, distribution should serve the interests at hand.

When we say concerning pilgrimage offerings and Eid sacrifices that it is recommended to eat a third and give a third in charity, this applies only when there is no reason to favour one allocation over another. Otherwise, if the poor were numerous, we would recommend giving more than a third in charity. The same principle applies if those to whom one gives gifts outnumber the poor, and likewise to the portion one eats.

Where receipt is based on need or benefit, consideration must be given to need and benefit according to the actual circumstances. Inheritance is different: its shares are apportioned according to relationships of kinship that apply equally to those who possess them. The term “son” includes the old and the young, the strong and the weak. A son receives neither because of his need nor because of his benefit, but solely because of his kinship. For this reason, those within the same category receive equal shares.

In these other cases, however, receipt is based on need and benefit. Equal distribution among the categories therefore cannot be either obligatory or recommended. Rather, giving must be proportionate to need and benefit, just as the underlying entitlement depends on them. The conjunction “and” entails

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

Allah has made obedience to the Messenger obligatory upon everyone in nearly forty places in the Quran. Obedience to him is obedience to Allah: it is worshipping Allah alone, without partner. That is Allah’s religion—Islam. Whoever Allah has commanded people to obey—whether a scholar, ruler, parent or husband—is to be obeyed because obeying him constitutes obedience to Allah. If, however, he commands something contrary to obedience to Allah, he must not be obeyed.

A parent or husband may command something permissible and thus be obeyed. The same applies to a ruler when he gives an order to a scholar who knows that it constitutes disobedience to Allah, and to a scholar when he gives someone a ruling that the questioner does not know to be contrary to Allah’s command: the person obeying them is not disobeying Allah. But if he knows that it is contrary to Allah’s command, then obeying them in that matter constitutes disobedience to Allah.

For this reason, several scholars have reported a consensus that a scholar may not follow another scholar’s opinion once he has exercised independent judgment, examined the evidence, and clearly recognized the truth brought by the Messenger. In that case, he may not follow someone whose view contradicts it; there is no disagreement about this. But may he follow another scholar’s opinion when he is himself capable of examining the evidence?

There are two views on this. The position of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad and others is that he may not. Permission to do so has been attributed to Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. This is a well-known issue, and some have also attributed this view to Ahmad.

but the person who reported this did not understand Ahmad’s position, as explained elsewhere. According to the majority of scholars, someone unable to examine the evidence may follow a scholar’s opinion. The qualifications of those permitted to do so involve distinctions and disagreements that are beyond the scope of this discussion.

The point here is that the following of others forbidden by the revealed texts and scholarly consensus consists in setting a contrary opinion against the word of Allah and His Messenger, whoever holds that opinion. Allah Most High says:

“On the Day the wrongdoer bites his hands, saying, ‘If only I had taken a path with the Messenger!’”

“‘Woe to me! If only I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!’”

“‘He led me away from the Reminder after it had come to me.’ Satan has always been a betrayer of mankind.”

“And the Messenger will say, ‘My Lord, my people have abandoned this Quran.’”

He Most High also says:

“On the Day their faces are turned about in the Fire, they will say, ‘If only we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!’”

And the passage continues as far as His words:

“and curse them with a great curse.”

He Most High also says:

“When those who were followed disown those who followed them, and they see the punishment, and all ties between them are severed.”

And the passage continues as far as His words:

“The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who calls out to what hears nothing but cries and shouts. Deaf, dumb and blind, they do not understand.”

Thus, He mentions how those who were followed in disobedience to Allah will disown their followers. He mentions this after saying:

“Your God is one God.”

The one God is the One who is worshipped and obeyed. Whoever obeys

someone he follows in contravention of this has a share in this condemnation. Allah Most High says:

“We have enjoined upon man care for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness.”

And the passage continues as far as His words:

“But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. Yet keep their company courteously in this world, and follow the way of those who turn to Me.”

Then He addresses mankind, telling them to eat what is lawful and good on earth and not to follow Satan’s footsteps in contravention of this. Satan commands only evil and indecency, and that they say about Allah what they do not know, declaring, “This is forbidden and that is lawful,” or making other statements about Allah without knowledge, concerning matters of fact and conduct. As Allah Most High says:

“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, ‘This is lawful and that is forbidden.’”

Then, when these people who speak about Allah without knowledge are told:

“Follow what Allah has revealed,” they say, “Rather, we follow what we found our fathers following.”

They have no knowledge; they merely follow their predecessors, adhering to what they have grown accustomed to and been brought up upon.

Then He addresses the believers specifically, saying:

“O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.”

“He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which a name other than Allah’s has been invoked.”

Thus, He commands them to eat the good things He has provided for them, because they are the intended recipients of His provision. Here He does not stipulate that it be lawful

because He has forbidden only what He mentioned, so everything else is lawful for them. As for mankind generally, He has commanded them to eat what is lawful and good on earth. Yet He has made things lawful only for believers; He has made nothing lawful for disbelievers. Lawfulness is therefore conditional upon faith. Whoever does not use His provision to help him worship Him has had nothing made lawful for him, even though He has not forbidden it either. Thus, it cannot be said that Allah has either made it lawful for them or forbidden it. He has only forbidden the Jews what He mentioned in Surah al-An‘ām.

For this reason, in Surah al-An‘ām and elsewhere, He condemns those who forbid what He has not forbidden, as when He says:

“Say, ‘Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?’”

Then He says:

“And to the Jews We forbade every animal with claws.”

Then He, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you,’”

and the verses that follow.

In Surah al-Nahl, He says:

“And to the Jews We forbade what We related to you before,”

and the rest of the verse. He states that He forbade these things because of their transgression, saying:

“For the wrongdoing of the Jews, We forbade them good things which had been lawful for them.”

He also says:

“Thus We recompensed them for their transgression.”

All of this supports the more correct of the scholars’ two views: this prohibition remains binding upon them after Muhammad was sent, and is lifted only by following him. It is a punitive prohibition imposed for their wrongdoing and transgression. Their wrongdoing and transgression have not ceased; rather, they have increased and become more grievous, making them still more deserving of punishment.

Moreover, Allah Most High spoke of this prohibition after Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent, to make clear that He had forbidden only the things He specified. Had that prohibition been lifted, He would not have mentioned it as an exception.

Moreover, a prohibition can be lifted only by His making the thing lawful, and He has made the eating of good things lawful only for believers, saying:

“There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten,”

and the rest of the verse. He also says:

“Livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you, without your being permitted to hunt.”

And He says:

“They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say, ‘Good things have been made lawful for you,’”

through to His words:

“The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them.”

This addresses the believers. Hence He says:

“The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you,”

then says:

“And your food is lawful for them.”

If whatever has been made lawful for us were also lawful for them, there would have been no need for this statement. His words, “And your food is lawful for them,” do not include what has been forbidden to them, just as His words, “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you,” do not include things forbidden to us which they regard as lawful, such as game hunted within the Sacred Precinct and animals slaughtered with the invocation of a name other than Allah’s.

Does their food which has been made lawful for us include what has been forbidden to them but not to us—for example, when they slaughter camels? There is a well-known disagreement over this. The established position in Mālik’s school—which is also one of the two positions in Ahmad’s school—is that it is forbidden. The position of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, and the other position in Ahmad’s school, is that it is lawful.

Is the legal basis that they did not intend a valid ritual slaughter, or that it is not part of their food? There is disagreement over this.

{إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْتُمُونَ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ وَيَشْتَرُونَ بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا أُولَئِكَ مَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ إلَّا النَّارَ وَلَا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَلَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ}
 فَهَذَا حَالُ مَنْ كَتَمَ عِلْمَ الرَّسُولِ وَذَاكَ حَالُ مَنْ عَدَلَ عَنْهَا إلَى خِلَافِهَا وَالْعَادِلُ عَنْهَا إلَى خِلَافِهَا يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ مَنْ قَلَّدَ أَحَدًا مِنْ الْأَوَّلِينَ والآخرين فِيمَا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ خِلَافُ قَوْلِ الرَّسُولِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ صَاحِبًا أَوْ تَابِعًا أَوْ أَحَدَ الْفُقَهَاءِ الْمَشْهُورِينَ الْأَرْبَعَةِ أَوْ غَيْرِهِمْ. وَأَمَّا مَنْ ظَنَّ أَنَّ الَّذِينَ قَلَّدَهُمْ مُوَافِقُونَ لِلرَّسُولِ فِيهَا قَالُوهُ فَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ سَلَكَ فِي ذَلِكَ طَرِيقًا عِلْمِيًّا فَهُوَ مُجْتَهِدٌ لَهُ حُكْمُ أَمْثَالِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُتَكَلِّمًا بِلَا عِلْمٍ فَهُوَ مِنْ الْمَذْمُومِينَ.
translated_text:
If they slaughter an animal for a Muslim, is the ruling the same as when they slaughter it for themselves? There is disagreement over this. There are also two opinions on whether they may slaughter sacrificial animals, provided they belong to those whose slaughtered meat is lawful. Both opinions are reported from Ahmad: prohibition is Mālik’s position, while permissibility is the position of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī. If the slaughterer is Jewish, two grounds for prohibition then arise concerning the slaughter. This, however, is not the place to discuss these questions.

Then, after describing those who speak about Allah without knowledge, merely following their predecessors, He, glorified be He, described those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance Allah has revealed after He has made them clear to people in the Book. He said:

“Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and exchange it for a small price consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Resurrection nor purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.”

This is the condition of those who conceal the Messenger’s teaching; the former is the condition of those who turn away from it to what contradicts it. Those who turn away from it to what contradicts it include anyone who follows an earlier or later authority in something he knows contradicts the Messenger’s words, whether that authority is a Companion, a Successor, one of the four renowned jurists, or anyone else.

As for someone who believes that the authorities he follows agree with the Messenger in what they say, if he has reached that conclusion through a scholarly method, he is exercising independent scholarly judgment and is subject to the same ruling as others like him. But if he speaks without knowledge, he is among those who are blameworthy.

original_text:
وَمَنْ ادَّعَى إجْمَاعًا يُخَالِفُ نَصَّ الرَّسُولِ مِنْ غَيْرِ نَصٍّ يَكُونُ مُوَافِقًا لِمَا يَدَّعِيه؛ وَاعْتَقَدَ جَوَازَ مُخَالَفَةِ أَهْلِ الْإِجْمَاعِ لِلرَّسُولِ بِرَأْيِهِمْ؛ وَأَنَّ الْإِجْمَاعَ يَنْسَخُ النَّصَّ كَمَا تَقُولُهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَالرَّأْيِ فَهَذَا مِنْ جِنْسِ هَؤُلَاءِ. وَأَمَّا إنْ كَانَ يَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ الْإِجْمَاعَ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَصٍّ لَمْ يَبْلُغْنَا يَكُونُ نَاسِخًا لِلْأَوَّلِ. فَهَذَا وَإِنْ كَانَ لَمْ يَقُلْ قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا فَهُوَ مُجْتَهِدٌ فِي ذَلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ لَهُ فَسَادَ مَا قَالَهُ كَمَنْ عَارَضَ حَدِيثًا صَحِيحًا بِحَدِيثٍ ضَعِيفٍ اعْتَقَدَ صِحَّتَهُ فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ حَقًّا لَكِنْ يُبَيِّنُ لَهُ ضَعْفَهُ وَذَلِكَ بِأَنْ يُبَيِّنَ لَهُ عَدَمَ الْإِجْمَاعِ الْمُخَالِفِ لِلنَّصِّ أَوْ يُبَيِّنَ لَهُ أَنَّهُ لَمْ تَجْتَمِعْ الْأُمَّةُ عَلَى مُخَالَفَةِ نَصٍّ إلَّا وَمَعَهَا نَصٌّ مَعْلُومٌ يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ النَّاسِخُ لِلْأَوَّلِ فَدَعْوَى تَعَارُضِ النَّصِّ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ بَاطِلَةٌ وَيُبَيِّنُ لَهُ أَنَّ مِثْلَ هَذَا لَا يَجُوزُ؛ فَإِنَّ النُّصُوصَ مَعْلُومَةٌ مَحْفُوظَةٌ وَالْأُمَّةُ مَأْمُورَةٌ بِتَتَبُّعِهَا وَاتِّبَاعِهَا وَأَمَّا ثُبُوتُ الْإِجْمَاعِ عَلَى خِلَافِهَا بِغَيْرِ نَصٍّ فَهَذَا لَا يُمْكِنُ الْعِلْمُ بِأَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ خَالَفَ ذَلِكَ النَّصَّ.
 وَالْإِجْمَاعُ نَوْعَانِ:
 قَطْعِيٌّ. فَهَذَا لَا سَبِيلَ إلَى أَنْ يُعْلَمَ إجْمَاعٌ قَطْعِيٌّ عَلَى خِلَافِ النَّصِّ.
 وَأَمَّا الظَّنِّيُّ فَهُوَ الْإِجْمَاعُ الإقراري والاستقرائي:
 بِأَنْ يَسْتَقْرِئَ أَقْوَالَ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَلَا يَجِدُ فِي ذَلِكَ خِلَافًا أَوْ يَشْتَهِرُ الْقَوْلُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَلَا يَعْلَمُ أَحَدًا أَنْكَرَهُ فَهَذَا الْإِجْمَاعُ وَإِنْ جَازَ الِاحْتِجَاجُ بِهِ
translated_text:
Anyone who claims a consensus that contradicts a text from the Messenger, without a text supporting his claim, and believes that those forming the consensus may oppose the Messenger on the basis of their own judgment, and that consensus abrogates a text—as some speculative theologians and proponents of personal opinion maintain—is of the same kind as these people.

If, however, he believes that the consensus indicates the existence of a text that has not reached us and that abrogates the earlier text, then, although his position is unsound, he is exercising independent scholarly judgment in this matter. The error in his position should be explained to him, just as with someone who counters an authentic hadith with a weak hadith that he believes to be authentic. Although his assertion is not true, its weakness should be explained to him.

This is done by showing him that no consensus contrary to the text exists, or by explaining that the Muslim community has never agreed to depart from a text unless it possessed a known text which its members knew abrogated the earlier one. Thus, the claim that a text and consensus conflict is false. It should also be explained to him that such a thing is inadmissible: the texts are known and preserved, and the community is commanded to seek them out and follow them. As for establishing a consensus contrary to them without a supporting text, it is impossible to know that every single Muslim scholar has opposed that text.

Consensus is of two kinds:

Definitive consensus: there is no way to establish a definitive consensus contrary to a text.

As for presumptive consensus, this comprises consensus established through tacit acknowledgment and consensus inferred from surveying scholarly opinions: one surveys the scholars’ statements and finds no disagreement on the matter, or a statement in the Quran becomes widely known and one knows of no one who has objected to it. Such a consensus, although it may be cited as evidence,

original_text:
فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ تُدْفَعَ النُّصُوصُ الْمَعْلُومَةُ بِهِ لِأَنَّ هَذَا حُجَّةٌ ظَنِّيَّةٌ لَا يَجْزِمُ الْإِنْسَانُ بِصِحَّتِهَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَجْزِمُ بِانْتِفَاءِ الْمُخَالِفِ وَحَيْثُ قَطَعَ بِانْتِفَاءِ الْمُخَالِفِ فَالْإِجْمَاعُ قَطْعِيٌّ. وَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ يَظُنُّ عَدَمَهُ وَلَا يَقْطَعُ بِهِ فَهُوَ حُجَّةٌ ظَنِّيَّةٌ وَالظَّنِّيُّ لَا يُدْفَعُ بِهِ النَّصُّ الْمَعْلُومُ لَكِنْ يُحْتَجُّ بِهِ وَيُقَدَّمُ عَلَى مَا هُوَ دُونَهُ بِالظَّنِّ وَيُقَدَّمُ عَلَيْهِ الظَّنُّ الَّذِي هُوَ أَقْوَى مِنْهُ فَمَتَى كَانَ ظَنُّهُ لِدَلَالَةِ النَّصِّ أَقْوَى مِنْ ظَنِّهِ بِثُبُوتِ الْإِجْمَاعِ قَدَّمَ دَلَالَةَ النَّصِّ وَمَتَى كَانَ ظَنُّهُ لِلْإِجْمَاعِ أَقْوَى قَدَّمَ هَذَا وَالْمُصِيبُ فِي نَفْسِ الْأَمْرِ وَاحِدٌ. وَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ نُقِلَ لَهُ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ فُرُوعٌ وَلَمْ يَتَعَيَّنْ صِحَّتُهُ فَهَذَا يُوجِبُ لَهُ أَنْ لَا يَظُنَّ الْإِجْمَاعَ إنْ لَمْ يَظُنَّ بُطْلَانَ ذَلِكَ النَّقْلِ وَإِلَّا فَمَتَى جُوِّزَ أَنْ يَكُونَ نَاقِلُ النِّزَاعِ صَادِقًا وَجُوِّزَ أَنْ يَكُونَ كَاذِبًا يَبْقَى شَاكًّا فِي ثُبُوتِ الْإِجْمَاعِ وَمَعَ الشَّكِّ لَا يَكُونُ مَعَهُ عِلْمٌ وَلَا ظَنٌّ بِالْإِجْمَاعِ وَلَا تُدْفَعُ الْأَدِلَّةُ الشَّرْعِيَّةُ بِهَذَا الْمُشْتَبَهِ مَعَ أَنَّ هَذَا لَا يَكُونُ فَلَا يَكُونُ قَطُّ إجْمَاعٌ يَجِبُ اتِّبَاعُهُ مَعَ مُعَارَضَتِهِ لِنَصٍّ آخَرَ لَا مُخَالِفَ لَهُ وَلَا يَكُونُ قَطُّ نَصٌّ يَجِبُ اتِّبَاعُهُ وَلَيْسَ فِي الْأُمَّةِ قَائِلٌ بِهِ بَلْ قَدْ يَخْفَى الْقَائِلُ بِهِ عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ.
 قَالَ التِّرْمِذِيُّ:
 كُلُّ حَدِيثٍ فِي كِتَابِي قَدْ عَمِلَ بِهِ بَعْضُ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ إلَّا حَدِيثَيْنِ: حَدِيثَ الْجَمْعِ؛ وَقَتْلِ الشَّارِبِ. وَمَعَ هَذَا فَكِلَا الْحَدِيثَيْنِ قَدْ عَمِلَ بِهِ طَائِفَةٌ وَحَدِيثُ الْجَمْعِ قَدْ عَمِلَ بِهِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ.
translated_text:
cannot be used to set aside known texts, because it is presumptive evidence whose validity one cannot affirm with certainty: one cannot be certain that no dissenting opinion exists. Where the absence of dissent is certain, the consensus is definitive. But where one merely considers dissent unlikely, without certainty, the evidence is presumptive. Presumptive evidence cannot override a known text. It may, however, be cited as evidence and given precedence over evidence of lesser probability, while stronger presumptive evidence takes precedence over it. Thus, whenever one considers the meaning indicated by the text more probable than the existence of consensus, one gives precedence to the text’s meaning. Whenever one considers the consensus more probable, one gives precedence to it. In reality, only one position is correct.

If subsidiary rulings on the matter have been reported to him, but the authenticity of the report has not been established, he must refrain from presuming a consensus unless he considers that report unsound. Otherwise, whenever he allows that the person reporting disagreement might be truthful or might be lying, he remains uncertain whether consensus exists. With such uncertainty, he has neither certain nor presumptive knowledge of a consensus. Scriptural evidence cannot be set aside on the basis of something so uncertain.

Yet such a situation does not actually arise: there can never be a consensus that must be followed while conflicting with another, otherwise unopposed text. Nor can there ever be a text that must be followed without anyone in the Muslim community upholding it. Rather, those who uphold it may be unknown to many people.

Al-Tirmidhī said:

“Every hadith in my book has been acted upon by some scholars, except two: the hadith on combining prayers and the hadith on putting the wine-drinker to death.”

Nevertheless, both hadiths have been acted upon by a group of scholars. The hadith on combining prayers has been acted upon by Ahmad and others.

original_text:
وَلَكِنْ مَنْ ثَبَتَ عِنْدَهُ نَصٌّ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ قَائِلًا بِهِ وَهُوَ لَا يَدْرِي:
 أَجْمَعَ عَلَى نَقِيضِهِ أَمْ لَا؟ فَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ رَأَى دَلِيلًا عَارَضَهُ آخَرُ وَهُوَ بَعْدُ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ رُجْحَانَ أَحَدِهِمَا فَهَذَا يَقِفُ إلَى أَنْ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُ رُجْحَانُ هَذَا أَوْ هَذَا فَلَا يَقُولُ قَوْلًا بِلَا عِلْمٍ وَلَا يَتَّبِعُ نَصًّا. . . 
(١)
 مَعَ ظَنِّ نَسْخِهِ وَعَدَمِ نَسْخِهِ عِنْدَهُ سَوَاءٌ لِمَا عَارَضَهُ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ نَصٍّ آخَرَ أَوْ ظَنِّ إجْمَاعٍ وَلَا عَامًّا ظَنُّ تَخْصِيصِهِ وَعَدَمِ تَخْصِيصِهِ عِنْدَهُ سَوَاءٌ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ الدَّلِيلُ سَالِمًا عَنْ الْمُعَارِضِ الْمُقَاوِمِ فَيَغْلِبُ عَلَى ظَنِّهِ نَفْيُ الْمُعَارِضِ الْمُقَاوِمِ وَإِلَّا وُقِفَ. وَأَيْضًا فَمَنْ ظَنَّ أَنَّ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْإِجْمَاعِ يُحْتَجُّ بِهِ فِي خِلَافِ النَّصِّ إنْ لَمْ يَتَرَجَّحْ عِنْدَهُ ثُبُوتُ الْإِجْمَاعِ أَوْ يَكُونُ مَعَهُ نَصٌّ آخَرُ يُنْسَخُ الْأَوَّلُ وَمَا يَظُنُّهُ مِنْ الْإِجْمَاعِ مَعَهُ.
 وَأَكْثَرُ مَسَائِلِ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ الَّتِي يَحْتَجُّونَ فِيهَا بِالْعَمَلِ يَكُونُ مَعَهُمْ فِيهَا نَصٌّ فَالنَّصُّ الَّذِي مَعَهُ الْعَمَلُ مُقَدَّمٌ عَلَى الْآخَرِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّحِيحُ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ كَتَقْدِيمِ حَدِيثِ عُثْمَانَ:
 
{لَا يَنْكِحُ الْمُحْرِمُ}
 عَلَى حَدِيثِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ وَأَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ.
وَأَمَّا رَدُّ النَّصِّ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْعَمَلِ فَهَذَا بَاطِلٌ عِنْدَ جَمَاهِيرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فِي مُخَالِفِ الْإِجْمَاعِ:
 هَلْ يَكْفُرُ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ.
translated_text:
But someone who has established the authenticity of a text, yet knows of no one who upholds it and does not know whether a consensus has formed against it, is like someone who encounters two conflicting pieces of evidence without yet knowing which carries greater weight. He must suspend judgment until it becomes clear which outweighs the other. He must neither express an opinion without knowledge nor follow a text … (1) when he considers its abrogation and its non-abrogation equally likely because of another text or a presumed consensus that he considers to conflict with it. Nor may he follow a general text when he considers it equally likely that its scope has or has not been restricted. The evidence must therefore be free of any countervailing evidence of equal weight: he must consider the absence of such countervailing evidence more probable. Otherwise, judgment must be suspended.

Furthermore, who would suppose that a consensus of this kind could be invoked against a text unless he considered the existence of that consensus more probable, or had another text abrogating the first, supported by what he believed to be a consensus?

In most matters in which the scholars of Medina invoke established practice as evidence, they also have a text supporting their position. The text supported by established practice takes precedence over the other. This is the correct position within the school of Ahmad and others—for example, giving precedence to the hadith of ʿUthmān:

“A person in ihrām must not marry,”

over the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, and similar cases.

As for rejecting a text solely on the basis of established practice, the overwhelming majority of scholars regard this as invalid. Scholars have differed over whether someone who opposes consensus thereby becomes a disbeliever; there are two views.

And the correct conclusion is that whoever opposes a consensus known with certainty becomes a disbeliever, just as whoever opposes a revealed text becomes a disbeliever by abandoning it. However, this occurs only in matters in which a revealed text is known to be established. As for knowing with certainty that consensus exists on a matter for which there is no revealed text, this does not occur. Where consensus is not known with certainty, one cannot declare someone a disbeliever for opposing it. Thus, consensus and the revealed text constitute two proofs, like the Quran and the Sunnah.

Scholars have also differed over whether consensus constitutes conclusive or presumptive evidence. The correct conclusion is that consensus established with certainty is conclusive, while consensus established presumptively is presumptive. And Allah knows best.

A verse similar to this one has been mentioned in Surah al-Mā’idah. In Surah al-Zukhruf, He says:

“Even if I bring you better guidance than what you found your forefathers following?”

This applies to anyone to whom it has been made clear that another position offers better guidance than the position with which he was raised: he must follow it. As He says:

“Follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

And He says:

“Hold firmly to them, and command your people to follow the best of them.”

And He says:

“Those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it.”

In matters of belief, one must follow the better of two positions. No one may hold a position while believing that the opposing position is better. When someone is given a choice between two actions, one of which is better, that action remains preferable. Even if he is permitted to perform the less preferable action, he must believe the other to be better and hold it dearer than the lesser one. This is following what is best.

وَإِذَا نَقَلَ عَالِمُ الْإِجْمَاعِ وَنَقَلَ آخَرُ النِّزَاعَ:
 إمَّا نَقْلًا سُمِّيَ قَائِلُهُ؛ وَإِمَّا نَقْلًا بِخِلَافٍ مُطْلَقًا وَلَمْ يُسَمَّ قَائِلُهُ فَلَيْسَ لِقَائِلٍ أَنْ يَقُولَ نَقْلًا لِخِلَافٍ لَمْ يَثْبُتْ؛ فَإِنَّهُ مُقَابِلٌ بِأَنْ يُقَالَ وَلَا يَثْبُتُ نَقْلُ الْإِجْمَاعِ بَلْ نَاقِلُ الْإِجْمَاعِ نَافٍ لِلْخِلَافِ وَهَذَا مُثْبِتٌ لَهُ وَالْمُثْبِتُ مُقَدَّمٌ عَلَى النَّافِي.

 أَوْ لِعَدَمِ الدَّلَالَةِ قِيلَ لَهُ:
 وَنَافِي النِّزَاعِ غَلَطُهُ أجوز؛ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ يَكُونُ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ أَقْوَالٌ لَمْ تَبْلُغْهُ؛ أَوْ بَلَغَتْهُ وَظَنَّ ضَعْفَ إسْنَادِهَا وَكَانَتْ صَحِيحَةً عِنْدَ غَيْرِهِ؛ أَوْ ظَنَّ عَدَمَ الدَّلَالَةِ وَكَانَتْ دَالَّةً فَكُلُّ مَا يَجُوزُ عَلَى الْمُثْبِتِ مِنْ الْغَلَطِ يَجُوزُ عَلَى النَّافِي مَعَ زِيَادَةِ عَدَمِ الْعِلْمِ بِالْخِلَافِ. وَهَذَا يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهِ عَامَّةُ الْخِلَافِ؛ فَإِنَّ عَدَمَ الْعِلْمِ لَيْسَ عِلْمًا بِالْعَدَمِ لَا سِيَّمَا فِي أَقْوَالِ عُلَمَاءِ أُمَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الَّتِي لَا يُحْصِيهَا إلَّا رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ؛
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ:
 مَنْ ادَّعَى الْإِجْمَاعَ فَقَدْ كَذَبَ؛ هَذِهِ دَعْوَى الْمَرِيسِيَّ وَالْأَصَمِّ؛
 وَلَكِنْ يَقُولُ:
 لَا أَعْلَمُ نِزَاعًا وَاَلَّذِينَ كَانُوا يَذْكُرُونَ الْإِجْمَاعَ كَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَبِي ثَوْرٍ وَغَيْرِهِمَا يُفَسِّرُونَ مُرَادَهُمْ: بِأَنَّا لَا نَعْلَمُ نِزَاعًا وَيَقُولُونَ هَذَا هُوَ الْإِجْمَاعُ الَّذِي نَدَّعِيه. فَتَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْإِجْمَاعِ الَّذِي قُوبِلَ بِنَقْلِ نِزَاعٍ وَلَمْ يُثْبِتْ وَاحِدٌ
translated_text:
If one scholar reports a consensus and another reports disagreement—whether naming the scholar who held the dissenting view or merely reporting disagreement without naming anyone—it is not sufficient to say, “The report of disagreement is unsubstantiated.” For the reply would be, “The report of consensus is likewise unsubstantiated.” Indeed, the person reporting consensus denies the existence of disagreement, while the other affirms it, and affirmation takes precedence over denial.

If someone says, “The person reporting disagreement may have erred in affirming it, either because the chain of transmission is weak or because the statements cited do not indicate disagreement,” the reply is: “The person denying disagreement is even more liable to error. There may be opinions on the issue that have not reached him. Or they may have reached him, but he considered their chains of transmission weak, while others found them authentic. Or he may have thought the statements did not indicate disagreement when they did.” Every error possible for the person affirming disagreement is also possible for the person denying it, with the additional possibility of being unaware of the disagreement altogether. This applies to disagreements generally: lack of knowledge is not knowledge of nonexistence, especially regarding the opinions of the scholars of Muhammad’s community—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which none but the Lord of all worlds can fully encompass.

For this reason, Ahmad and other scholars said: “Whoever claims consensus has lied. This is the claim of al-Marīsī and al-Asamm. Rather, one should say, ‘I know of no disagreement.’” Those who used to cite consensus, such as al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Thawr, and others, explained that they meant, “We know of no disagreement,” and would say, “This is the consensus we claim.”

It is thus clear that a consensus of this kind, countered by a report of disagreement, when neither has been established

translated_text:
cannot be cited as evidence. If someone finds neither the report affirming disagreement nor the report denying it more persuasive than the other, he likewise has no grounds to give the claimed consensus precedence over the scriptural text, or the text precedence over it. Rather, he must suspend judgment, since neither carries greater weight for him. If he finds the report affirming disagreement more persuasive, he considers it most likely that no consensus contradicts the text, and he acts upon that text.

In assessing this, he considers those reporting consensus and disagreement. Someone known frequently to claim consensus when the facts are otherwise is not on the same footing as someone who has never been known to affirm a consensus subsequently shown not to exist. Likewise, someone known to err only rarely when reporting disagreement is not on the same footing as someone known to make frequent mistakes.

When two people independently report disagreement, neither having taken his report from the other, their reports establish that disagreement exists. Claims of consensus are different: even if several people concur in reporting consensus, this establishes only that they know of no disagreement. This applies to those who affirm disagreement over combining the three and those who deny it. Moreover, most of those affirming disagreement cite an authentic report that cannot be dismissed, while those denying it have nothing that invalidates it.

Many later jurists—or most of them—say that they are unable to derive all the rulings of Islamic law from the Messenger’s teachings. They therefore treat their imams’ statements as equivalent to the Messenger’s statements and follow their authority. Undoubtedly, many people need to follow the authority of scholars concerning matters that arise which they cannot understand independently. Among those who follow the path of spiritual aspiration, worship, poverty, and Sufism are some who treat their shaykh

translated_text:
in the same way. Indeed, he may even regard him as infallible, taking guidance for his spiritual path only from him rather than from the Messenger—even though learning to follow the spiritual path from the Messenger is easier than learning the disputed points of law. For the spiritual path consists in following the way Allah and His Messenger have commanded in matters of belief, worship, and character. All of this is clearly explained in the Book and Sunnah, for it is like nourishment that the believer cannot do without.

Thus, all the Companions knew how to follow the spiritual path through the guidance of the Book and Sunnah and the teachings conveyed from the Messenger. They had no need to consult the jurists among the Companions about this. Nor did disagreements arise among them concerning it, as they did over certain questions of jurisprudence whose answers were unknown to most of the Companions. They would discuss fatwas and legal rulings, and some of them would seek fatwas on these matters.

As for the obligatory and recommended deeds performed by someone seeking nearness to Allah, all of them learned these from the Book and Sunnah, for the Quran and hadith are filled with such teachings. Even if one of them spoke about this without himself citing a source, his words or their meaning would be transmitted from Allah and His Messenger. One of them might utter a word of wisdom, and you would find it reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This accords with what has been said in explanation of His words:

“Light upon light.”

Yet many devoted to worship and asceticism have turned away from seeking the prophetic knowledge through which they could learn the way of Allah and His Messenger. Consequently, they have needed to follow the authority of a shaykh.

There are also matters concerning the spiritual path over which the shaykhs have disagreed. Yet the Book and Sunnah contain texts indicating the correct view that most people following this path can understand. Matters concerning the spiritual path are like matters of creed: all are explicitly addressed in the Book and Sunnah. The speculative theologians disagreed only when they turned away from the Book and Sunnah; once they ventured into religious innovations, disagreements arose. The same applies to the path of worship: most disagreements concerning it arise only because people turn away from the prescribed path, fall into religious innovations, and consequently disagree among themselves.

Likewise, disagreements in jurisprudence arose because the Prophet’s explanations of the Law were not clear to them. Such disputes, however, concern its finer points; they do not disagree over its major matters. The Companions themselves disagreed over some of these questions, but they did not disagree over matters of creed or the path to Allah by which a person becomes one of Allah’s righteous friends who are brought near to Him.

For this reason, when most shaykhs needed guidance on legal questions—such as marriage, inheritance shares, purification, the prostrations for forgetfulness, and similar matters—they followed the authority of the jurists, because deriving these rulings from the texts was difficult for them. As for matters such as reliance upon Allah, sincerity, and asceticism, they exercised their own judgment. Those among them who followed the Messenger were correct, while those who departed from his guidance were mistaken.

Will in general, however, is an attribute shared by all animals: there is no animal without a will. These people shared the desire to worship, but differed over whom they worshipped and how they worshipped. Thus Allah described Christian monasticism in the Quran as something they had invented, and condemned the polytheists for the acts of worship and prohibitions they had invented. These were more numerous than their invented beliefs, for they were generally ignorant in matters of belief, and so their innovations in that sphere were fewer. Hence, the closer people were to the Messenger, the less grave their innovations were, and these concerned doctrines. Among the Successors and their followers, there was no one who worshipped through dancing and devotional listening, although there were Khārijites, Mu‘tazilites, and Shiites among them. There were those who denied divine decree, but none who invoked divine decree as a justification.

Most of the numerous innovations that arose among later devotees, ascetics, the poor, and Sufis did not exist in the time of the Successors and their followers. By contrast, the doctrines of those who introduced doctrinal innovations appeared during the age of the Companions and the Successors. This shows that the specious reasoning behind those doctrines was stronger and their adherents more rational. As for the innovations of these later groups, their adherents are more ignorant and further removed from following the Messenger. People have recognized that those philosophers are not Muslims, yet these people claim to be Allah’s allies while making statements that only someone whose unbelief exceeds that of Jews and Christians would make.

Many of them—or most of them—do not realize that this contradicts the Messenger. Indeed, one group among them believes that the People of the Portico fought the Messenger and that he approved of their doing so. Others believe that the Messenger was commanded to go and greet them and ask them to supplicate for him, but that they refused him permission to enter, saying, “Go to those to whom you were sent.” They claim that he then returned to his Lord, who commanded him to humble himself and say, “Your humble servant has come to greet you.” They then comforted him and permitted him to enter.

Despite holding this monstrously unbelieving doctrine—which no Jew or Christian who acknowledges him as Allah’s Messenger to the unlettered would hold—they say that the Messenger approved of their conduct and acknowledged it, and that he acknowledged them as Allah’s chosen intimates. They claim that Allah addresses them without the Messenger’s mediation and has given them no need of him, just as some of a king’s intimates have no need of his ministers. They cite the account of al-Khidr and Moses as evidence, whereas it is evidence against them, not in their favour, in many respects that have been explained at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
the latter, who in turn display a degree of arrogance, miserliness, and hardness of heart not found in the former. Thus, the former resemble Christians, while the latter resemble Jews. Allah Most High has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path,
the path of those You have blessed—not those who have incurred Your wrath, nor those who have gone astray.”

Consequently, many of their leading spiritual masters eventually came to contemplate Allah’s oneness in lordship and to affirm divine decree, which encompasses everything in existence. They regarded complete absorption in this contemplation, with the disappearance of the distinction between good and evil deeds, as the highest spiritual station. Beyond it lay only what they called “oneness,” which is a form of the indwelling and union professed by Christians. Yet they fear expressing this openly and treat it as a concealed secret.

Some of them say that this was al-Hallāj’s spiritual vision, and that he was killed only because he divulged a secret that should not have been divulged.

If, in addition, one of them has learned from speculative theologians or others who argue for divine decree and regard everything as proceeding from a single will—with no love, hatred, pleasure, displeasure, or joy, but merely different objects of that will, so that its relation to reward is called pleasure and its relation to punishment is called displeasure—then, with this spiritual vision, he no longer retains any distinction. They call this “gathering” and “overwhelming absorption.”

Then there are people who uphold this distinction, but for their own sake and desires, not as worship and obedience to Allah. The one who neglects these duties resembles a monk, while the self-serving person resembles someone who seeks nothing but this world. The former is an innovator, and the latter an evildoer.

translated_text:
He was also asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

“Is someone correct in saying, ‘The scriptural texts do not cover a hundredth of the Sharia’? Does he mean an unambiguous text that admits no alternative interpretation, or transmitted wording that admits different interpretations?

“Are those Zāhirīs who reject analogical reasoning and declare it invalid correct? What evidence do they have for that?

“What do they mean by the term ‘text’?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This statement was made by a group of proponents of speculative theology and juristic opinion, such as Abū al-Maʿālī and others, and it is mistaken. Rather, the correct position, held by the majority of Muslim imams, is that the scriptural texts cover most of the rulings governing people’s actions.

Some maintain that they cover all such rulings. Those who deny this do so only because they have not understood the meanings of the texts of general scope—the words of Allah and His Messenger—or how comprehensively they encompass the rulings governing people’s actions. For Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with concise yet comprehensive speech. He would utter a comprehensive statement of general scope constituting a universal proposition and a general principle encompassing numerous categories, which in turn encompass countless individual instances. It is in this way that the scriptural texts encompass the rulings governing people’s actions.

translated_text:
An example of this is that Allah prohibited khamr, but some people thought that the term applied only to grape juice. Some of them therefore prohibited nothing else, while others also prohibited certain intoxicating drinks made by infusion. This is the position held by some jurists of Kufa. Abū Hanīfa prohibits grape juice that has become strong and frothy; this, in his view, is khamr. He also prohibits cooked grape juice unless two-thirds of it has evaporated; once two-thirds has evaporated, he no longer prohibits it. He prohibits uncooked date infusion, but considers it lawful if it has been cooked even slightly. These three intoxicating drinks are not khamr in his view, although they are forbidden. As for other infused drinks, he prohibits only the amount that causes intoxication. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, however, agreed with the majority that every intoxicant is forbidden, whether in small or large quantities. The leading scholars among Abū Hanīfa’s followers issued fatwas to this effect, and this was also the position adopted by Abū al-Layth al-Samarqandī.

Some scholars prohibited every intoxicant through analogical reasoning, extending either the term or the ruling. This approach was followed by a group of jurists among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, who thought that the prohibition of every intoxicant rested solely on analogy concerning either terminology or the ruling.

The correct position, held by the great imams, is that the khamr mentioned in the Quran encompasses every intoxicant. Thus, the prohibition of every intoxicant is established by the scriptural text of general scope

Authentic statements from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) also establish the prohibition of every intoxicant. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is reported to have said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ā’isha (may Allah be pleased with her) reports that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.”

The two Sahīhs also report from Abū Mūsā that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked:

“We have a drink made from honey called al-bit‘, and a drink made from sorghum called al-mizr?”

The narrator said that he had been endowed with concise, comprehensive speech, and he replied:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden.”

There are other hadiths as well, which would take too long to recount. Accordingly, the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and foods, such as intoxicating hashish, is established by the scriptural text. This text encompasses drinking every kind of intoxicant, whatever its ingredients: grains, fruits, the milk of horses, or anything else.

Those who thought that the text applied only to grape wine said that it did not explain the ruling on these other intoxicants—which are more abundant in the world than grape wine—and that their prohibition was instead established by analogy. translated_text:
grape wine at all; Medina had no grapevines, but only date palms, so their khamr was made from dates. When khamr was prohibited, they poured away those date-based drinks, knowing that they were forbidden khamr. This establishes that, in their usage, the word khamr was not restricted to grape juice. It makes no difference whether this was already its meaning in their language, so that it encompassed [other drinks] (1), or whether they understood its broader scope through the Messenger’s explanation (peace and blessings be upon him), for he explains what Allah intends. The Lawgiver uses language as people do in customary usage, sometimes employing a word more broadly than its linguistic meaning, and sometimes more narrowly.

Likewise, according to most scholars, the term maysir (gambling) encompasses playing backgammon and chess. It also encompasses sales involving uncertainty, which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) prohibited, because they involve the gambling that constitutes maysir. Gambling means that a person’s money is taken while he runs the risk of receiving nothing in return. Examples include buying a runaway slave, a straying camel, habal al-habala, and similar things that the buyer may or may not obtain. Accordingly, the term maysir in the Book of Allah Most High encompasses all of these. The authentic report in Sahīh Muslim states:

“The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade sales involving uncertainty.”

This encompasses every transaction involving such risk, including selling fruit before it shows signs of ripening, selling unborn animals in the womb, and other such transactions.

The same applies to the term ribā (usury), which encompasses every prohibited form of ribā
